This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for calculating the ground state of a given operator, defined by $(-\Delta_{d})^{s}$ where $s\geq 0$, acting on the domain $\mathbb{B}^{d}$ with $d\geq 2$. We demonstrate that as the training sample size increases towards infinity, it exhibits convergence towards a compact, convex subset of its phase space, denoted as $\mathcal{B}_{d,s$. This subset lies within a specific space of functions possessing certain growth restrictions and is comprised of sequences that converge towards the ground state of the given operator. The conclusion was derived using a combination of techniques from spectral theory and deep neural networks. This finding, in particular, extends previous work referenced in \cite{CNS, Ngo}. The resulting outcome may provide a theoretical explanation for the remarkable success of deep neural networks in solving certain differential equations and functions. Furthermore, the ability to define the ground state using a compact, convex subset of a given space may facilitate the development of confinement algorithms. In a subsequent study, we will explore a convergence rate theorem for neural networks initializing their weights within this subset. The current study, however, focuses on establishing the initial outcome.

The intricacy of the human nervous system makes studying C. Elegans, a simpler organism with well-documented behavioural and structural biology, an attractive option for modelling and simulating neural activity. This work presents a new model that uses a mass action-based approach for neural communication, closely mimicking the biological synapse mechanism of C. Elegans. This numerical simulation model for C. Elegans can be reconfigured as a complex network, allowing for the study of neural interactions through network principles. Building on this model, researchers have explored the patterns of neural connectivity in the context of a network representing the organism's brain. Key topological features of this network were identified and a preliminary model is proposed to explain its formation, considering the developmental process of the organism. Lastly, the potential applications of this model for organoid development and rehabilitation therapies are discussed. A strong Gelfand pair (G,H) is defined by a group G and subgroup H, 
with every irreducible character of H resulting in a multiplicity-free 
character of G. Specifically, we identify the strong Gelfand pairs of SL(2, 
p) when considering dihedral groups D4(p) as its subgroup. 
This investigation yields twenty possible combinations. 
Using a reliable combinatorial approach, we rule out nine of these combinations. 
As a result, we pinpoint eleven valid strong Gelfand pairs and determine the 
corresponding irreducible modules for each. 

Key to our proof is the establishment of a one-to-one correspondence 
between the eigenvectors of specific 2x2 matrices, which encode the character 
tables of Sl(2, p) and D4(p). This novel approach is both computationally 
efficient and universally applicable, also enabling the identification of 
multiplicity-free but non-strong Gelfand pairs. 

Our methodology is exemplified through a detailed analysis of the case 
p=5, which is further illustrated through various practical applications, 
including the derivation of irreducible modules for eleven specific Sl(2, 5) 
subgroups. Our findings are also corroborated by Doob plots, which visually 
illustrate the distinctness of the identified modules. 
Lastly, a comprehensive summary is provided of the known results from 
pre-existing studies on this subject. 

This research is a foundational precursor to a forthcoming paper, which will 
explore similar problems in the context of Gl(2, p). 

We are proud to announce that, to our knowledge, this study represents 
the most comprehensive characterization of irreducible modules for Sl(2, 
p) characterized to date. 

In addition to its theoretical significance, the character tables and irreducible 
module tables calculated in this investigation may prove useful to other 
researchers and practitioners in related fields. 
This is particularly evident when dealing with p = 2, 3, 5, 7, 11. 
We have made an effort to make the tables easy to read by including clear 
descriptions of the characters involved. 
The data has been made available for download on an online repository. 
https://github.com/LeeLing/Sl2p_charactergithub. 
The knowledge gained in this investigation may also prove adaptable to the 
Gl(2, p) context, as will be detailed in our forthcoming follow-up paper.

This thesis proposal outlines my research objectives, which focus on these concerns, as well as initial findings, which reveal that the Isabelle Archive exhibits characteristics typical of scale-free networks, as evidenced by the distribution of node in-degrees in its dependency graph. These include insights on author productivity and the satisfaction of reuse criteria within the Isabelle Archive. The tools and methods described also facilitate the exploration of content by topic, as demonstrated using selected topics related to Isabelle. Ultimately, the work outlined in this thesis aspires to contribute valuable insights and experiences to the Isabelle community, as well as to foster collaboration among researchers, reviewers and the Isabelle toolchain, as facilitator. A new class of rotating black brane solutions, including all possible rotational parameters, have been constructed in an arbitrary number of dimensions. These rotating black branes are flat in topology at their horizons, yet due to the influence of the dilaton field, they do not conform to either flat or (anti)-de Sitter asymptotic behaviors. We've analyzed their physical properties by applying a method that uses the counterterm, which was inspired by AdS/CFT correspondence. This has allowed us to calculate mass and angular momentum, and we have determined the temperatures, electric potentials, and entropies at the horizons, thereby confirming the first law of thermodynamics. The Bayesian mass model, however, is able to accurately predict unknown regions on the other side of the 'nuclear pocket' while achieving similar levels of precision, demonstrating its advantages over traditional methods. The Bayesian mass model has the ability to seamlessly incorporate theoretical predictions and data from future experiments, allowing it to make predictions based on constantly evolving knowledge of the nuclear model. One of the key problems originating from communication complexity, known as the promise set disjointness problem, holds crucial importance in numerous applications. The scenario revolves around k players with subsets S1 through Sk, and it's guaranteed that the intersections between any two sets lie empty; this guarantees the exact output of a disjunctive function for these sets as zero. The challenge involves determining if the intersection of any two sets is non-empty when all other disjointness conditions are met. The analysis focuses on single-element (heavy hitter) and multi-element (heavy subset) intersections. The concept of heavy hitters, where a subset with the highest frequency experiences significant interest, is addressed here. The study of heavy hitters encompasses determining which elements appear most frequently within the input stream. The primary contribution of this paper lies in deriving lower bounds on memory and sketch size for heavy hitter and set disjointness problems in the context of streaming algorithms. The findings reveal that heavy hitter algorithms require at least Ω(n/(h+1)) memory to identify heavy hitters with probability 3/4, and Ω(n/(h^2 - 1/n)) for heavy subsets. Conversely, a sketch of size O(n) is possible with high probability in worst-case scenarios, but this may compromise on probability - falling to 1/4 as the goal - in such cases. The analysis further demonstrates that this new bound is significantly better than previously established ones for heavy subset problems. The study also shows that disjointness problems demand an inherent lower bound of Ω(n) on memory, and the previous works have therefore been suboptimal. We investigate the momentum dependence of the static magnetic susceptibility in
Heisenberg magnets, particularly within the context of the paramagnetic phase of
the antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model, where it is described through the
Matsubara sum of elementary magnetic moments. By comparing this approach with
experimentally measurable values derived from inelastic neutron scattering, we
determine the relationship between the correlation length and the momentum
dependence of the magnetic susceptibility. We then apply this framework to
study the renormalization of parameters within the O(3) nonlinear sigma model,
which describes the same phase. The results of our analysis, obtained via
perturbation theory, reveal how the susceptibility evolves at critical points
related to the O(3) nonlinear sigma model. We find that at the Wilson-Fisher fixed
point, the susceptibility exhibits momentum dependence with a Fourier transform
of the correlation function that is proportional to $\xi^2/p^2$. However, this
conventional form holds true only at the weak coupling limit; strong coupling effects
introduce deviations from this prediction. Furthermore, our analysis of the
conventional model yields an anomaly in the momentum dependence of the
susceptibility as the model approaches the criticality, which is consistent with
previous theoretical predictions. We compare our results to computational findings
obtained from quantum Monte Carlo simulations of the square and cubic lattices, where
the correlation length is calculated via the variational method in the middle layer. 
Strong coupling effects are found to introduce a momentum dependence of the
susceptibility that is not accounted for within the conventional limit of the
Matsubara sum. The computed correlation lengths are also compared with predictions
derived from the conventional limit, which holds true in the case of the square
lattice but not for the cubic lattice, particularly at the critical correlation length. 
The found discrepancies emphasize the necessity of accounting for the momentum
dependence of the magnetic susceptibility, particularly in the context of systems
exhibiting enhanced susceptibility compared to the universal momentum
dependence of the O(3) nonlinear sigma model. The identified discrepancy between
the computable and predicatable results of the O(3) nonlinear sigma model may be
attributed to the failure of the conventional limit of the Matsubara sum for the
elementary magnetic moments to accurately represent the true momentum
dependence of the magnetic susceptibility, which is a distinct characteristic of
the quantum critical fluctuations present in the antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model.

Building on Sodemann and Fu's theory of the nonlinear Hall effect established in 2015, 
a semiclassical framework where it arises from Bloch electrons' anomalous velocity as a geometric property,
a broader theory is presented, encompassing correlated and disordered systems. 
At one extreme, within the wavefunction framework, the nonlinear Hall effect is shown to be equivalent to a measure of curvature in the entire band, 
not just high-energy states. 
At the other extreme, within the Green's function formalism, the nonlinear Hall effect is shown to be equivalent to the sum of odd parity terms in a Taylor expansion of the band's susceptibility. 
As a result, the nonlinear Hall effect is sensitive to the gaps created by topological features such as topological insulators, Weyl semimetals, and topological flat bands. 
Furthermore, the theory is applied to correlated systems by examining the t-J model on the honeycomb lattice and the canonical symmetry-protected topological model, 
where it is found that the nonlinear Hall effect can be a direct probe of dynamic or thermal correlation functions. 
Finally, the theory is applied to charge-density-wave systems, where it is found that the nonlinear Hall effect can be a means of detecting the topological features of the gap. 
Thus, the nonlinear Hall effect is revealed to be a powerful means of examining the electronic structure of correlated systems. 
In conclusion, the nonlinear Hall effect is suggested as a means of examining the electronic structure of disordered and correlated systems, 
as well as potential applications in the identification of topological features in these systems.

The phenomenon of the Pauli Exclusion Principle manifests itself when low-temperature 2D harmonic oscillator traps hold fermions at the ground state. As a result, the lack of interaction between fermions leads to the formation of Pauli crystals. This research aims to understand this occurrence by using statistical mechanics to determine the energy and dimensions of a non-interacting arrangement of ultra-cold fermions, combining two theories - fermion degeneracy and harmonic oscillator treatment. This unification of perspectives provides a more complete and reliable explanation for the characteristics of Pauli crystals. Based on this new understanding, we have derived an improved formula for calculating the dimensions of Pauli crystals, ensuring consistency across all possible fermion configurations within the trap. Additionally, we have confirmed that the Pauli crystals' arrangement of spin-aligned fermions constitutes the ground state of an attractive ferromagnetic Fermi gas, in line with the ideas previously discussed in the literature. Using a novel method, we have also derived an improved formula for calculating the energy of the Pauli crystals arrangement of spin-aligned fermions. This new formula surpasses previous predictions based on fermion degeneracy theory, showing improved accuracy. On the other hand, the Pauli crystals' arrangement of spin-aligned fermions, as well as those in opposite spins, do not exhibit any tendency towards attractive ferromagnetic or repulsive Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer behavior, respectively. Ultra-cold fermion arrangements, as studied in this research, hold potential as a suitable backdrop for exploring the theoretical concepts underlying quantum ferromagnetism and same-sex superfluidity within the context of ultra-cold quantum matter's study. A significant advantage of this new approach lies in the simplicity and reliability of the formulae derived for the Pauli crystals' energy and dimensions, making it a solid foundation for further theoretical and experimental investigations. Furthermore, we have derived an improved formula for calculating the chemical potential in 2D fermion degeneracy, as well as the critical fermion population for the onset of pair formation in a quasi-two-dimensional attractive attractor gas. Additionally, we have determined the formulae for the pairing gap within the quasi-two-dimensional attractive attractor gas, as well as the width of the superfluid coherence wave, known as a soft mode. These new formulae, though mathematically simple, exhibit high accuracy and consistency across all possible fermion population levels, thus far surpassing the accuracy and consistency of the well-known formulas derived by Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer for the similar phenomenon

To attain this goal, our research focuses on developing an end-to-end deep network that emulates the robust visual processing pathways in the vertebrate retinal visual system. This system features distinct pathways - one through the retina's ON-type pathways and another through OFF-type pathways - which, when combined, enable robust edge detection in various lighting conditions. Our RetinaHelper network replicates this biological structure by introducing a novel feature fusion module to enhance the network's ability to handle lighting-related tasks. Additionally, our research introduces a new retinal-like structure for image representation, called the RetinaHelper Layer (RHL), which can be integrated with numerous pre-trained networks to improve their robustness to lighting-related conditions. Through comprehensive testing, our system has demonstrated superior performance in resisting not only light exposure but also other common image corruption techniques. Our research further confirms that the specific arrangement of pathway structures in the retina may hold significance not only for light exposure but also for other image degradation scenarios, such as noise, rain, and image compression. Furthermore, our RetinaHelper module can be utilized as an efficient data augmentation technique to enhance the resistance of pre-trained networks to light exposure. Our team is currently developing a method to optimize the design parameters of wide-field X-ray telescopes with the goal of minimizing the number of Monte Carlo simulations needed to explore the complex design space. By assuming the presence of 4 focal plane detectors, our approach involves optimizing various design parameters including mirror prescriptions, shell displacements, detector placement, and tilt. By initially modeling higher-order polynomial terms as perturbations to an existing Wolter I optic design, we can utilize Monte Carlo simulations to generate trial analytic functions representing spatial resolution on an arbitrary focal surface. This leads to a notation and tool development for efficiently performing Monte Carlo simulations of polynomial mirror prescriptions, which enables the symbolic representation of polynomial coefficients. This novel approach enables the determination of these coefficients via the solution of a large set of linear equations using a single set of Monte Carlo simulations, assuming the presence of a predefined set of polynomial prescriptions. This represents the current state of our methodology development. Our next step will involve an in-depth investigation of this methodology, particularly with regard to its applicability to the specific case of the STO II X-ray telescope. This is a large, 5-meter diameter instrument featuring four shells, with a planned overall height of nearly 10 meters. Each shell is to be coated with a thin layer of gold, although the presence of a missing hole within the first shell may require the use of a specialized optics design. Our approach involves investigating the feasibility of utilizing this particular optic design, with the goal of minimizing the number of shell disruptions and associated losses in terms of usable signal. Our findings will be presented in further detail.

Researchers have been investigating constraint screening, a technique that can expedite the solution process for large-scale unit commitment problems by reducing the number of unnecessary constraints. Current constraint screening methods rely on optimizing load and generation, but this approach tends to be conservative and leaves a considerable percentage of constraints intact. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a machine learning-based model to predict costs given load inputs, enabling more effective optimization and constraint screening in unit commitment problems. By incorporating cost perspectives and machine learning, the proposed model outperforms conventional approaches, significantly reducing computational time across various scenarios. Furthermore, this work lays the groundwork for machine learning-based constraint screening in multi-period demand response applications. Detailed evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed model in this context. Compared to conventional methods, the proposed model achieves a substantial 75 percent reduction in computational time with a minimal 0.01 percent error margin when evaluated using actual data from the RTESM. Measurements of magnetization were performed on polycrystalline and single-crystalline 
samples of $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$, under pressures of up to 2 GPa, allowing for the creation 
of a temperature-pressure phase diagram for the material. Compression was found to have a 
minor effect on the N\'eel temperature, which increases at a rate of 1.5 K/GPa. At pressures 
above 1.3 GPa, the material undergoes a structural phase transition into a phase of lower 
symmetry. This transformation remains unchanged over an extended pressure range and 
involves no change in the magnetic ordering temperature. The magnetic phase transition in 
$\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ exhibits greater pressure dependence than that of other materials with the 
same honeycomb structure geometry, rendering it a promising system in which to study 
the relationship between valence bond and magnetic ordering. Furthermore, the findings 
for $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ are compared with those for Na$_2$IrO$_3$, as well as Tl$_2$RhO$_3$. 
Detailed examination of X-ray diffraction data confirmed that the material retains its 
hexagonal symmetry up to the highest measured pressures, thereby excluding 
explanation for the material's magnetization response based on magnetic field-induced 
orientation changes of the spins in the hexagonal planes. Instead, the findings suggest 
that the magnetization is driven by alignment of the spins that are interplanar. Moreover, 
the findings reveal the material's magnetization to be sensitive to unaligned irreducible 
magnetic domains within polycrystalline samples, as well as to any magnetic field 
orientation variation with respect to the crystallographic axis. The findings for $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ 
are consistent with recently proposed theoretical explanations for magnetization in this class of 
materials with the honeycomb geometry. As such, they provide further support for 
the underlying theory of magnetism and offer a promising approach to realizing a 
magnetization response free from any crystallographic constraint. Moreover, the findings 
open the way for investigating the relationship between spin orientation and crystallographic 
orientation in other magnetically ordered honeycomb lattice materials. Future studies 
should also explore the pressure-dependent properties of Na$_2$IrO$_3$, as well as Tl$_2$RhO$_3$,

Researchers frequently apply synthetic control techniques to determine the effect of treatment on a single treated entity within data sets that span multiple periods. The goal of synthetic control is to create a weighted average of units without treatment that mimics the treated entity's pre-intervention outcome trajectory. Initially, the weights used in synthetic control calculations are derived by correlating pre-intervention outcomes of the treated entity with those of units without treatment. It has been discovered, however, that traditional estimation techniques can be inconsistent. To resolve this challenge, this paper introduces a novel analytical framework, which formalizes the process of making causal inferences and estimating the effect of treatment on the treated. The new framework enables the reutilization of units previously considered unsuitable for the purpose, thereby ensuring that the estimated weights are consistent. The treated entity's outcomes can be contrasted with those of the synthetic control in the post-intervention period to create a time series. By employing techniques from the field of time-series analysis, this enables the estimation of the net impact of treatment on the treated unit. The author's own demonstrations of this method, which incorporate variables from the case of the Compa\`{o}re in Francophone countries, reveal improved results when compared to the existing literature. The proposed new approach has been incorporated into the 'SynthControl' R package, which also includes additional complementary estimators. The added estimators, which are also present in the literature, are different from those previously discussed. They are: the covariance shift-reweighting method, which recalculates the weights using a convergent iterative algorithm; the unknown variance method, which relies on a large number of units and time periods; and the k-fold method, which divides the treated entity's trajectory into distinct sections and applies the synthetic control estimation technique to each section. The 'SynthControl' package can be accessed via its dedicated repository at GitHub: https://github.com/michaellopes/synth_control. The package's documentation, which includes a rendered version of this paper, can be found at the following URL: https://mhlopes.github.io/synth_control/. Additionally, the authors have also made available at https://mhlopes.github.io/synth_control/index.html.html a pre-compiled version of the 'SynthControl' R package for Windows users. Additionally, the correct linear combination transformation was identified and used to link the generalised system to a specific type of Darboux variable problem. However, traditional methods that rely on average operations (like averages or means) often struggle when dealing with diverse data such as images. This is because these methods struggle to effectively propagate information from known categories to unknown ones, and can lead to subpar performance. One potential solution is to leverage graphs where models like GCN operate on them, but there's a significant issue here - these methods require large-scale multi-category classification datasets, which isn't what few-shot learning is all about. This work introduces a novel graph-based few-shot learning approach called GFC, which starts off by creating a global graph of data samples and classes where neighbors are defined by class labels. Then, a GCN-like operator is applied to classify new classes using only a few samples. This is where the GFC method diverges from other graph-based methods, as it uses a unique loss function that's tailored to few-shot learning. Unlike other few-shot learning techniques that rely on averages, GFC uses a GCN-like operator to leverage the information of known categories to enhance performance on new ones. This is particularly shown to be beneficial as the few-shot protocols we use keep the graph structure of known categories intact but destroy the one for the new categories, which is why information propagation becomes all the more important here. Interestingly, our findings show that the benefits of this approach increase significantly when fewer samples are available. When tested on the Omniglot and MiniImageNet datasets, our method, GFC, outperformed other baselines by a significant margin. The code for this has been made publicly available. Recent advancements in natural language processing have led to the development of models that integrate domain knowledge into their design, focusing on both performance and explainability. However, the need to protect these models against malicious attacks on the input has become a pressing concern due to the potential risks involved. A particular type of model, called a Neural ODE, is inherently resistant to such attacks simply by virtue of following a continuous equation that describes the evolution of the input over time. Previous research demonstrated that incorporating adversarial robustness into Neural ODE models could be achieved by drawing on principles from control theory that ensure system stability. Building on this work, our study draws a direct connection between adversarial robustness and the principles of Lipschitz stability in Neural ODEs. This connection leads us to develop specific design criteria for Neural ODE models that satisfy this stability condition, including a novel method to determine the domain of legitimate inputs that such models can accurately predict. Our method also enables us to assess and compare the robustness of these models in terms of their likelihood of correct prediction within specified boundaries. Our software implementations of these designs are available for public use. 

As our research shows, natural robustness offers a compelling advantage, and we encourage the exploration of control-theoretic approaches to developing Neural ODE models that combine state-of-the-art performance, explainability, and defense against malicious attacks. We anticipate that future work will involve refining our designs to accommodate limitations, such as reducing their computational overhead in real-world applications. We conducted an initial assessment of this limitation and discovered that the trade-off between performance and security is inherently a trade-off, but one that can be closely approximated with minimal sacrifice of quality. Our study as a whole emphasizes the unique potential of Neural ODE models to deliver superior results across multiple dimensions. 

We began by examining the distinct characteristics of Neural ODE models that distinguish them from other adaptable architectures, such as residual and transformer-based designs. Our research reveals that Neural ODE models excel in terms of domain-specific knowledge, explainability, and natural robustness, and we encourage further exploration of control-theoretic design principles to integrate these models into applications while accounting for potential risks. Our study also identifies areas for improvement, such as reducing the computational overhead of our designs and integrating more advanced control-theoretic guidelines. Our connections to other architectures serve as a starting point for other research directions to be investigated. Our software implementations of these designs are documented in the repository at https://github.com/utek/adversarial-ode and include the latest developments.

The nonlocal conservation laws with flux functions defined through the convolution product have been successfully applied to model vehicular traffic. A key aspect of this model is that the interaction not only takes place in the vicinity of each vehicle but also extends over a certain range of neighboring vehicles. This article focuses on a nonlocal conservation law with a flux function $f(\varphi) = \frac{1}{2}(\varphi^2 - 1)$ and an arbitrary initial condition $h(x), $ with the goal of obtaining the well-known "camera model" equation $\partial_t h = (h - 1)\partial_x h.$ A fundamental question concerning this model is whether the solution $h(t,x)$ can develop singularities as $h(t,0).$ This question is crucial because if a singularity occurs, it would develop almost instantly, within a finite amount of time. This article proves that such a singularity indeed arises and provides estimates of the formation time and other key properties of the solution. A novel approach of "initial" estimates via the ADI method has been developed and introduced in this study. Furthermore, it was demonstrated that the model's solution can be represented as the viscosity solution of a first-order Hamilton-Jacobi equation containing entropies and singular measures. An approximate model with Dirac masses has been developed and compared with an existing approximate model due to Bernot, Carlen and Carmona. Detailed analyses of the differences between these models have been conducted and presented in this article. Lastly, numerical simulations have been performed to visualize the model's solution and compare it with the camera model and the Bernot-Carlen-Carmona model. These simulations are available for download at the mentioned website. Based on the obtained results, it may be recommended to use the Bernot-CC model as an approximation for the nonlocal camera model. Recent studies have suggested using total correlation to measure functional connectivity between brain regions as a more comprehensive metric compared to traditional methods such as correlation coefficients. However, the interpretation of total correlation along with its generality across different brain networks remains unclear. In order to address these questions, we first expanded the concept of total correlation to multiple variables and proved several key properties, including its non-negative nature. We then developed a simulation approach to estimate total correlation values from neuroimaging data and created random network models to analyze the effects of different variables. Furthermore, we defined and derived a mathematical formula to measure the stability of functional patterns within brain networks, known as sparsity. In order to investigate the characteristics of total correlation, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of functional connectivity patterns using resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from multiple groups of subjects. Our results showed significant regional differences in total correlation, both in amount and spatial organization, and revealed distinct patterns of total correlation between different brain networks, particularly in individuals with autism spectrum disorder. Additionally, we discovered a positive relationship between sparsity and age in certain brain networks. Overall, our findings demonstrate the utility and promise of total correlation as a means of characterizing functional connectivity patterns and exploring underlying neurobiological processes. We believe that total correlation has the potential to enrich our understanding of brain networks and related neurological phenomena.

As the scope of Gaussian processes widens, the availability of simple mathematical solutions dwindles, prompting the need for alternative methods. Monte Carlo simulations serve as an intermediary between automatic and symbolic methods by introducing a flexible, although probabilistic, method. Traditional Monte Carlo approaches can be computationally resource-intensive or impractically imprecise when determining confidence intervals. To mitigate these issues, we've developed a new approach, based on efficient Latin Hypercube samples, which offers an unprecedented compromise between accuracy and computational efficiency. Our improved Monte Carlo method has been successfully applied across multiple artificial test cases and real-world scenarios. Furthermore, this article is accompanied by a publicly accessible R package, named alcide, which facilitates implementation of the proposed approach. The R package's functionality can be further expanded through user-submitted additional functions. Furthermore, all the examples presented in this article are included in the package for ease of access and reproduction. The R package's permanent repository can be found at https://github.com/JuliaDGC/alcide. Additionally, a mirror repository for the R package can be accessed at https://docs.yorkdev.net/uncertaintyanalysis/uncertaintyanalyses/r Package/. 
This work forms part of the research conducted leading to the PhD thesis titled 'Gaussian Process Methods for Predicting Material Behaviour: Efficient Monte Carlo Sampling Methods' presented to the University of Cambridge.

This research demonstrates the utilization of the Spatial Finite Discrete Fourier Transform (SFDFT) method in modeling outdoor wireless communication featuring the scattering of waves via multiple reflectors. Noting that dipole antennas in outdoor settings often experience significant ground reflection, this work explores the implications of incorporating a single ground reflector into the models, with a focus on environments characterized by uniform terrain. To simplify computations, an approximate model based on first-order approximations is developed, which reduces the multi-path problem to a set of broadcast waves with delayed phases. These models can be leveraged to develop and refine antenna designs through optimization techniques. To illustrate this potential, the article describes a case in which spatial beamforming optimization was applied using the SFDFT method. Moreover, a related Fourier-based method is suggested as a possible approach for modeling the interaction of multiple dipole antennas in complex multi-path scenarios. Finally, the analysis is expanded to consider the case of polarized antennas, introducing a novel Fourier-based parameterization technique to facilitate efficient computations. Various simulations were conducted to validate the accuracy and practicality of the proposed models. These simulations involved calculating electromagnetic wave patterns in different spatial domains, determining parameters for optimal antenna performance, and estimating signal power levels in complex environments. To further verify the effectiveness of the Fourier-based modeling approach, additional sine-sweep signals were introduced, with corresponding results comparing the proposed models' performance to that of a conventional method. Consequently, the spatial Fourier transform was found to be an efficient and powerful tool for characterizing the electromagnetic wave patterns produced by arrays of antennas. Notably, the Fourier-based approach to modeling antenna arrays offers computational advantages over traditional methods, which often require a greater number of resources, even in cases involving complex co-prime structures. We have established the parameters for neutrino mixing, which allows us to design more effective investigations of newly opened avenues of research. By taking precise measurements, we can test our current understanding of three types of neutrinos, their mass relationships, and CP symmetry in the lepton sector. Long-range neutrino experiments are expected to play a crucial role in enhancing our knowledge of these phenomena. The results of the most recent findings from the OPERA, T2K, and NOvA collaborations are presented, along with an update on the JUNO and DUNE experiments. Furthermore, the prospect of utilizing underground detectors to probe low-scale leptonic arches is briefly discussed. The neutrino project is set to become one of the most Thrilling areas of research in particle physics over the next ten years. This review outlines the remarkable advancements that are anticipated or have the potential to occur, based on the advancements that have taken place, and what new research initiatives are being undertaken. These developments include the parameterization of neutrino mixing, the study of rare processes on very long distance scales, the exploration of low-energy rare annihilation modes of the neutrino, and the potential discovery of new physics beyond the well-established standard model of particle physics. The review is written in the knowledge that the time of its publication falls between the completion of Run III and the beginning of Run IV of the LHC, and before the JUNO and DUNE experiments report their results. These developments are conversely expected to be based on the latest available data, and to discuss in detail various open issues and challenges in the field. The review is divided into five parts. The first part covers current progress and future prospects for three types of neutrino flavor oscillations. The part two discusses the development of new long-distance neutrino experiments. The part three is dedicated to the exploration of lepton-scale physics. The part four is dedicated to the potential discovery of new particles and interactions beyond the well-established standard model of particle physics. The part five concludes with a brief discussion of the challenges and problems in the field. The review is an expansion of the speaker's invited talk at the 2018 LASSA Summer School. This paper addresses challenges in the spatiotemporal predictive learning approach, known as ST-PL, that uses short observed sequences to forecast future frames and is widely applicable. One of the significant obstacles in this area is identifying meaningful spatiotemporal features, and excessive variation among successive frames exacerbates long-term forecasting difficulties. The main goal of this research is to improve the forecast accuracy by reinforcing the connection between near and distant future predictions. We introduce a novel bidirectional generative modeling framework for ST-PL, combining the future and past generative networks in a single architecture. This method can be used with various future and past learning strategies. We test our approach with the Natural Action Units Recognition System challenge dataset, and achieve significant improvements in action gesture and facial expression prediction. The proposed framework outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in multi-frame forecasting tasks by a substantial margin, with absolute peak signal-to-noise-ratio increases of 5, 3, and 2 for future, past, and joint learning configurations, respectively. Furthermore, our approach enhances the future generative network's ability to produce realistic and detailed results by a large margin. Permutation decoding is a widely used technique that enables traditional decoding to be applied despite variations in code indices, using permutations to compensate for this shift. However, when employing permutation decoding in polar codes, which have previously been restricted to small system sizes due to this shift issue, the need for a new method to determine which permutations are valid is now crucial. In this research, a new approach to identifying valid permutations for permutation decoding in polar codes is introduced, requiring only O(n) time, regardless of the size of the code, and is therefore highly efficient even for large codes. A range of simulations demonstrate that the error rates of the proposed decoder are comparable to those of the best previously-known polar code decoders. Notably, the proposed decoder is the first to successfully decode polar codes of sizes up to 1024. A supplementary video providing further details on the implementation of the proposed decoder is also available. As an additional contribution, this research shares open-source code for permute-and-remap decoders, including permutation-based decoding variants, to facilitate comparisons of their performance. The code is stored on a public GitHub repository. Furthermore, a new permutation search algorithm, requiring only O(n) time, is introduced and implemented in the code to achieve optimal error-performance. The proposed algorithm is therefore highly efficient even for large codes. The research also introduces a novel error-correction method, known as list less-to-top, which is based on cutting off low-probability lists in the Galois metric and retaining the top-scoring options, producing near-optimal error-performance while being notably faster than other methods. A supplementary video providing further details on the implementation of the proposed less-to-top algorithm is also available. In addition to these contributions, the research presents a new method of applying permutation decoding to polar codes, which is based on applying a pre-determined set of rotations to the code index, and is therefore inherently fast and efficient. While this approach is simpler than the proposed permute-and-remap decoding method, it is also less effective, producing higher error-rates. We examine the link between the choice of image co-adding technique and the final image's point spread function. This involves identifying the characteristics of co-adding algorithms that yield co-added images with well-defined point spread functions. Our investigation centers on the following points:

  1. A clear illustration shows how linear co-adding techniques can produce linear point spread functions if and only if they preserve point sources, as demonstrated by the linear diffraction wavefront transformers.
  2. The concept of linear co-adding being equivalent to preserving point sources is not unique to image co-adding, as it also applies to wavefront transformers.
  3. A new definition of nonlinear co-adding is introduced, and two notable examples are discussed: first, the '4i - 1' algorithm, which maintains a linear point spread function; second, the '4i' algorithm, which does not.
  4. The '4i' algorithm is notable for preserving the twinkle effect, a characteristic that has significant implications for point source identification and correction.

  The effectiveness of our linear co-adding method is highlighted through its application to Hubble Space Telescope full-frame image "PFImage". This involves co-adding the center pixel of 27 full-frame images to produce a final image with minimal noise and a point spread function. Our analysis shows that the co-added image has a uniform noise level across the full field of view, with a point spread function that remains unchanged unless the co-adding weight deviates from this uniform level. Our findings suggest that the co-added image with this level of noise is the optimal representation of the object, free from the distortions associated with the diffraction wavefront. When applied to the HST full-frame image "PFImage", our co-adding method produces an image with higher signal-to-noise ratio compared to the original full-frame image. Additionally, the final image shows signs of underlying structure not present in the original full-frame image. This underlying structure is consistent across 25 out of 27 individual full-frame images, with the two exceptions likely the result of telescope degradation. These combined findings confirm our theoretical predictions and underscore the significance of this linear co-adding method. Generating synthetic cell instances realistically often requires intricate cell models accurately illustrating complex cell structures. Traditionally, this has been done using voxel-based approaches, which require often or exclusively using 3D volumetric data, or polygon mesh models, which can be imperfect due to potential gaps and holes. We introduce a new method to create level sets of signed distance functions that encapsulate a cell's topology, making it suitable for synthetic generation when paired with a trained neural network, which can learn a pattern linking input indices to level sets. Since level sets are defined across the entire 3D space, this method naturally handles cases where cell boundaries overlap by simply selecting the appropriate isovalue. We've found that it significantly outperforms existing voxel-based and mesh-based methods, also demonstrating comparable performance to a generative adversarial network approach when paired with a synthesis method for generating synthetic cells. Importantly, this technique allows users to easily investigate generated cells in detail by adjusting the isovalue to reveal the cell wall, membrane, or cytoplassistant. The code is available at https://github.com/nrl-ncc/LevelSetsForCellModelling.

This representation accurately captures turbulence's essence, characterized by the shift from one coherent structure to another. Our analysis yields exact expressions for the turbulent transport operator without employing simplifying assumptions. In the limit where spatial and temporal locality prevail, our operator reduces to the conventional estimate of turbulent transport as a diffusivity tensor, with its components being the integrated velocity field auto-correlation over time. However, this conventional estimate falls short in capturing the flow's intermittent nature and structural variations. As an alternative, we propose a spectral tensor decomposition of the correlation operator. Our method stands on its rigor and independence from spatial discretization assumptions. Moreover, in contrast to conventional estimates, our approach can effectively capture the flow's anomalies and patterns like vortex sheets and instabilities in vortex dynamics. Additionally, we have established a stochastic integral equation for turbulent transport that views the flow field as a random force acting on a passive scalar. Our findings and implementations using direct numerical simulation data show that turbulent transport properties can be better understood by exploring the spectra of the correlation tensors, which reveal the flow's intrinsic complexities. In the case of a rotating three-dimensional turbulence, our approach has revealed the linear and nonlinear cyclic patterns within the flow. Moreover, our approach has revealed the flow's dominant modes and cluster structures in the case of a transient growth of a mixing interface in an oscillating aero-dynamical obstacle and the prevalent linear and nonlinear patterns of the flow at the dominant modes in the turbulence. Moreover, our approach has effectively captured the flow's anomalies and patterns like vortex sheets and dynamic instability of the vortices in the flow. Our approach has also been validated by showing the exactness of the operator and the effectiveness of the tensor decomposition in capturing the flow's properties even at the level of the single hydrodynamic mode. Our study shows that the operator's spectrum changes significantly in the flow as the flow transitions from the intermittent state to the periodic state and from the periodic state to the intermittent state. Our approach has effectively been used to provide an exact expression for the turbulent transport operator in terms of the flow field statistics and to highlight the major shortcomings of the conventional estimates of the turbulent transport properties compared to the proposed exact expression and decomposition of the transport properties in the terms of the tensor decomposition of the correlation operator.

Within this investigation, the challenge of vehicle platooning with connected and automated vehicles is resolved through a differential game approach. This study explores various information network configurations, beginning with the 'leader-follower' model where each vehicle maintains a distance from its immediate predecessor. Additionally, the two-predecessor model is analyzed, in which a following vehicle's distance is regulated by both the preceding vehicles. These two information scenarios are evaluated to assess their respective advantages and drawbacks. Ultimately, the findings are intended to influence the development of vehicle platooning protocols with a focus on optimizing safety. Various simulation case studies are conducted to validate the theoretical outcomes and demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed safety protocols. These protocols are designed to guarantee stability within the studied differential game, thereby ensuring distance control. Furthermore, the existence of these differential game solutions is verified through a stable limit cycle. It is anticipated that the derived protocols will stimulate discussions regarding the application of these strategies in real-world platooning scenarios. While the current work concentrates on ensuring safety, future investigations will be directed towards developing strategies to achieve the fastest possible time. Various case studies are executed using plain matrices and MATLAB's optimal control toolbox to determine the most effective set of control parameters. Interestingly, it was discovered that the existence of multiple solutions coincides with the non-unicity of the optimal control parameters, which calls for further reinforcement learning investigations to identify the optimal control parameters. Lastly, the study explores the sensitivity analysis of the obtained results with respect to the pre-existing distance between the predecessor and predecessor vehicles. Several numerical case studies were executed, yielding the conclusion that the existing distance has a positive effect on the existence of the optimal control parameters. It is also worth mentioning that the various information network configurations, such as vehicle speed, sensor characteristics, and communication system capabilities may serve as potential sources of these distances. Consequently, the study's findings are versatile and can be applied to different platooning scenarios. Moreover, the existence and uniqueness of the optimal control parameters may be influenced by the specific configuration of the information network, thereby widening the scope of the proposed study. A comparative case study analysis is intended to identify the optimal control parameters based on various learning methods such as Newton's first-order and second-order methods, deep policy gradient, asynchronous policy optimization, cross-entropy loss, and actor-critic algorithm. The derived strategies and findings are anticipated to stimulate further investigations towards achieving the fastest possible time. A preliminary case study analysis revealed that the various learning methods have distinct optimal control parameters, which highlights the potential for optimizing the learning methods themselves

One of the widely applied optimization methods in machine learning is Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), which tackles optimization problems by iteratively selecting and computing gradients of small data subsets before updating the solution. When executed in parallel, SGD demands communication among involved processes at each iteration. Our innovation is a communication-optimizing approach for utilizing SGD to train neural networks, which aims to minimize communication during the training process. This strategy is based on the principle of delaying the exchange of information until necessary, thereby reducing the total communication required to achieve convergence on a given task. As an alternative to existing methods such as data synchronization, our technique bypasses the need for data transmission by deploying training operations on the trainer and data exchange only when necessary. As a result, this strategy is expected to offer substantial benefits, particularly for tasks requiring a large number of training steps and tasks without strict convergence guarantees. Our experimental findings confirm the potential for substantial communication reductions, with significant speed-ups projected (e.g., a 10-fold increase on tasks like image classification using Google's Colab). We have further developed an intuitive yet flexible training system to demonstrate the applicability of this approach to diverse deep learning applications trained on large datasets. Additionally to our method, we also devised strategies for optimizing the actual training computations. As a result of integrating these computations and system considerations, our approach allows for substantial performance improvements, ultimately leading to faster solution times. For instance, our technique for optimizing the actual training computations can reduce SGD execution times by as much as $3.4\times$ (on Google Colab with SGD optimization of image classification) and our overall communication-avoiding training framework can offer speed-up factors of $33\times$ (on Google Colab with SGD optimization of language modeling) and $57\times$ (on Intel Shark with image classification). Moreover, our technique allows for substantial speed-up even on systems lacking high-bandwidth GPU accelerators (e.g., a $3.4\times$ speed-up on Google Colab with SGD optimization of language modeling). As an additional benefit, our method for optimizing the actual training computations enables the use of lower-end GPUs (e.g., a $3.4\times$ speed-up on Google Colab with an NVIDIA K80 vs. the high-bandwidth Pascal GPU). On the other hand, FFT-based architectures reduce computational demands, but implementing the Fourier transform might require up to double the original processing resources. Nevertheless, combining the correlator function with the Fourier transform in a single step yields promising outcomes. In this context, a proposed FFT-correlator architecture is presented, capable of executing real-time corrections, modulating patterns, and sampling within compact field probes, thereby facilitating the efficient detection of subtle signals while minimizing additional hardware needs. A new scheme, the 'diagonalized' FFT-correlator, is also introduced, allowing the efficient inclusion of real-time corrections, while maintaining sensitivity to the desired signals. With the 'diagonalized' architecture, the required hardware resources can be halved, albeit at the cost of some signal processing speed. Additionally, implementing the scheme within compact field probes brings the benefit of on-site computing, thereby facilitating the efficient detection of signals, especially in the case of deep space interferometers. A new open-source tool is used to compare the proposed architecture with traditional correlators. Given the impending creation of massive radio interferometers, the required improvements to hardware and software are also evaluated. In the near future, the proposed architecture is likely to enhance the detection efficiency of radio telescopes, while awaiting the development of more advanced technologies to render the proposed system obsolete. According to our calculations, the proposed architecture is approximately two times more efficient than traditional correlators in terms of computational requirements. However, implementing the proposed architecture within compact field probes comes at a speed cost, ranging from 3 to 6 percent slowdown, which is nonetheless acceptable in the case of deep space detection. As the density of the sampling grid increases, both architectures converge towards achieving the desired signal processing sensitivity. Given the substantial reduction in hardware resources required by the diFFT scheme, implementing real-time corrections becomes a very appealing option. For several decades, the Markowitz framework has been used for in-depth portfolio analysis but it focuses solely on return analysis, overlooking the vital consideration of risk. Recent advancements in generative models such as conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (cGANs) hold potential to generate multiple samples of unlabeled financial time series data under specified conditions, thereby enabling the creation of multiple risk series given a specified risk level. This could facilitate simultaneous generation of return and risk series, allowing the circumvention of traditional Markowitz assumptions. Nevertheless, the conditional generative model is restricted by its reliance on perfect input data, and when provided with imperfect data, it is incapable of producing well-distributed risk series, a shortcoming that can be addressed by implementing an unsupervised variational autoencoder (VAE) based generative model. The latter's ability to produce undominated risk series given an arbitrary risk level, while avoiding extreme environmental risks, relies on a novel representation discontinuity preserving loss. The performance of the proposed model is demonstrated through experiments on actual stock data. The proposed model's results illustrate its capability to generate multiple risk series, each with varying levels of risk, and its potential to create a risk-return portfolio that is more resilient to environmental market risks. The proposed model's novel loss strategy facilitates the creation of a more stable risk series and the representation of risk through a specific latent variable, resulting in the creation of undominated risk series. The proposed model's efficacy is further validated by its ability to outperform established portfolio selection methods on actual historical stock data. The proposed model's pre-trained generative network can also be utilized for autocompletion, a capability that can be employed in the analysis of time series gaps or uncompleted data. The proposed model has the potential to enhance the performance of modern portfolio selection methods. The accompanying source code is available at https://github.com/amaneshtman/UniMarkowitz. The research described in this paper contributes to the understanding of generative models for unlabeled time series data analysis, and the associated code and model can be utilized in other applications of unsupervised time series analysis. The proposed model's novel loss function can be utilized in other representation learning-based time series analysis tasks. The research described in this paper is part of a larger Ph.D. thesis titled "Time series generative models: advancing modern portfolio theory's limitations." analyse online interactions, enabling them to make data-driven decisions when 
creating or sharing content. To facilitate future research, we present our findings

for future exploration into the various forms of content being created. By 
Demonstrating how our framework can be applied to diverse types of video

We establish that any hypergraph can be viewed as a composition of hypergraphs formed by a common tensor-based operation. This operation allows us to identify and create novel hypergraph classes, enabling us to calculate various properties and spectra for hypergraphs constructed in this way. We also obtain results on the spectra of hypergraphs by applying our tensor-based method, and demonstrate its utility by constructing cospectral hypergraph pairs for adjacency, Laplacian, and normalized Laplacian matrices. Furthermore, we show that hypergraphs formed by repeating a fixed tensor along specific paths within a larger hypergraph are equivalent to those formed by the tensor product of the hypergraphs corresponding to each path, and establish a relationship with hypergraph covers. We also present a new method for constructing hypergraph covers based on this representation and prove that hypergraphs formed by repeating the same hypergraph along the hyperedges of another hypergraph admit a factorization of their tensor product, and that this gives rise to a new hypergraph classes. We show that these classes are closed under subgraphs and that certain hypergraphs formed in this way have desirable spectral properties. Specifically, we construct hypergraphs with roots and collinear hyperedges with improved spectral properties. However, treating time as a categorical variable can introduce complications, particularly when appointments are missed or rescheduled due to events like the COVID-19 pandemic, which risks inducing bias. This paper demonstrates how the capabilities of confusion networks can be leveraged efficiently by representing them in a compact form suitable for use in dialogue management. In experiments, we have found that using confusion networks enhances task performance compared to the usual top N approach. In addition, we have introduced a new architecture for the confusion network that further enhances its effectiveness, one that can in fact outperform the best results previously achieved with top N hypotheses in the Switchboard benchmark. Despite the potential of confusion networks, they have been largely neglected due to the high computational demands required to decode them. To address this limitation, we have also investigated the feasibility of sampling the most likely hypotheses from the confusion network distribution, thereby allowing for a faster but approximated decoding of the confusion network, one that can match the performance of the full set of hypotheses. Our results show that this sampling approach can reduce decoding time by as much and even outperform the full set of hypotheses in the Switchboard benchmark. The proposed sampling method may also have applications in other areas such as natural language processing. This study is the first to show the promise of using confusion networks in dialogue management. Our analysis of decoding time required to achieve the same accuracy as the top N approach shows that a speedup of 4X to 5X over the top N method is achievable while achieving a similar accuracy. This speedup is appealing as it is complementary to previous methods aimed at reducing decoding time, one that uses instead a different trade-off between accuracy and speed. The proposed sampling method is also complementary to previous methods such as [14], [17]. Our analysis shows that the main factor contributing to the inefficiency of the confusion network method is the large number of hypotheses, one that can be alleviated by implementing a more efficient technique to sample hypotheses from the confusion network distribution, one that can reduce the sampling time in the log-linear model by about an order of magnitude. Notably, using optimal estimators does not necessitate full state tomography; in fact, we compare the results to those obtained from tomographic reconstructions using two different sets of projectors, demonstrating the latter's reduced precision. Furthermore, we leverage optimal estimators to assess and compare the performance of different noise models describing decoherence effects that arise during entanglement generation. Specifically, we evaluate the impact of independent noise on individual photons and noise correlated across the pair, revealing that the source of noise has a substantial effect on measurement precision. Following the success of frozen pre-trained models in continuing learning, numerous adaptive mechanisms have been developed to address the challenge of storing multiple versions of the model. In this study, a new approach is proposed to facilitate continued learning of image classification tasks through a single high-capacity frozen pre-trained model and a compact trainable backbone model. A small adjustable network, called the Mask Generator (MG), is introduced to control the shared parameters of the two models. MG enables the models to adapt rapidly to new tasks while preserving previously learned knowledge. An analysis of our method shows that it can be viewed as a special instance of latent variable models, where an adjustable encoder uses MG to control the shared parameters and task-specific information. We demonstrate that our method outperforms existing continued learning techniques on key datasets and present an innovative, efficient continued learning system. We also explore the use of MG in low-resource settings, such as mobile devices and embedded systems, and validate its efficacy in reducing system load. This paper introduces a general framework for the capacity region of a complex interference channel with interconnected user pairs, characterized by a collection of interconnected rectangles, with each rectangle defined by paired rates of mutual information. While this formula is computationally challenging, it provides valuable insights into the nature of interference channels and facilitates more accurate modeling of interference in specific channel scenarios, such as when inputs follow discrete ergodic Markov processes. Furthermore, numerical analysis confirms that taking the interference structure into consideration can yield better performance in suboptimal coding schemes, like the interference avoidance code. We have also discovered that the interference structure is fully captured by the degrees of mutual information, and that these values have specific upper limits for the interference channel with a single transmitter, thereby laying the groundwork for a future proof-of-concept coding scheme based on these mutual information degrees. Each rectangle within this framework corresponds to a coding approach involving a sequence of discrete states representing the channel state, with each state associated with a rectangle facet. We have analyzed the complexity of implementing these coding strategies using conventional coding methods, such as variable-length coding, turbo coding, and binary coding with interference avoidance. We have also introduced a symbolic dynamics method for converting the discrete states into a one-dimensional space and developed the necessary tools for this conversion. We have further investigated the relationship between the degrees of mutual information and the necessary codice length in various channel scenarios, with numerical results confirming that our proposed coding approach can offer superior performance over time. We have extended this framework to the case of multiple transmitters and multiple receivers, with each rectangle becoming a potentially complex polyhedron in this more general scenario. We have observed that our simple coding approach can achieve asymptotically optimal performance when there are two transmitters and one receiver. We have further explored this framework in the context of the Rayleigh block-fading interference channel, with numerical results indicating that our coding approach can be optimal in this scenario as well. We have also developed the interference structure for this Rayleigh block-fading channel and discovered that coding for interference has a meaningful physical structure. The threat of homicide death tolls has raised concerns worldwide and demands attention from researchers and government officials, a trend exemplified by the high numbers in Brazil, where homicides have become the primary cause of death for people in the 15-39 age group and the third overall leading cause of death.  In the broader South American context, Brazil ranks third for its homicide death toll behind only Venezuela and Colombia.  In assessing the consequences of violent acts on community levels, understanding the relationship between the aggressor and victim is a key area of study.  A key challenge in this investigation lies in measuring victim characteristics, as official records are often unavailable or unreliable.  In this study, we develop three separate methodologies to estimate the characteristics of homicide victims in Brazil, all of which demonstrate that victims tend to be younger and have lower socioeconomic statuses than their aggressors.  We find our results to be consistent with studies from the United States and other countries that have also explored this topic.  By accounting for victim demographics, our models experience increased accuracy and performance, and our results suggest a strong correlation between victim and aggressor characteristics.  According to our study findings, incorporating victim estimates into predictive frameworks for homicide risk reduces average annual prediction errors by 15 and 20 percent for logistic and Poisson regression analyses, respectively.  In terms of victim influence on homicide prediction, our study indicates that considering victim demographics is at least twice as important as considering the aggressor's prior criminal record.  A comprehensive collection of statistical software code and the supplementary data used in this study have been made publicly available.  This resource is intended to facilitate replication of our results as well as support future research on the topic.  In addition, our study's findings are intended to contribute to the development of more effective public policies to prevent violence.  To this end, the dataset used in this research will be made publicly available to other researchers and government officials to aid in the formulation of more precise predictions and strategies for dealing with a problem that continues to plague Brazilian communities. We propose InDistill, a novel model compression approach, combining the principles of knowledge distillation and channel pruning to effectively transfer critical information flow from a powerful teacher model to a more efficient student model. Unlike previous techniques that collapse this information, InDistill leverages layer-wise pruning of the teacher's intermediate stages, aligning their widths with those of the student, thereby enabling direct information distillation without an intermediate encoding step. To facilitate knowledge transfer, we employ a curriculum learning strategy that prioritizes layer-wise difficulty and critical learning periods. Through these advancements, InDistill significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving enhanced results on a range of benchmarks, including ImageNet and CIFAR-100. Importantly, our method surpasses channel pruning alone by more than 10%, highlighting its superior performance. Human vocal synchronization in social interactions provides valuable information about a person's cognitive behaviors. In this paper, we investigate the effectiveness of unsupervised techniques for detecting entrainment patterns in vocal interactions and, subsequently, predicting corresponding cognitive and behavioral characteristics. We developed an innovative method for the unsupervised clustering of acoustic signals with varying lengths, using both linear and non-linear representations of the data. The first involved predicting clinical diagnoses of autism spectrum disorder and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, while the second focused on forecasting developmental trajectories in at-risk infants. Our comprehensive evaluations, including data analysis and performance evaluation across the aforementioned frameworks, demonstrated the efficacy of our proposed method in identifying entrainment patterns and predicting relevant outcomes. Moreover, our findings suggest that certain aspects of vocal synchronization may serve as early indicators of developmental risks. Our proposed testbed, SyROF, is designed to facilitate the development of
cooperative robot systems, making it easily accessible for both undergraduate
and graduate students to implement robotic swarms in a timely manner. To achieve
this goal, we developed SyROF, an innovative testbed that features a user-friendly,
high-level programming environment supporting the Timed Input/Output Automata
(TIOA) paradigm. This versatile tool boasts the following distinctive features: 
1) A simple, portable framework for robot control based on the TIOA concept, 
2) A synchronized mechanism for executing transparent, real-world robot commands
3) A comprehensive, visual tool for monitoring robotic activities and performance 
evaluation. To demonstrate the SyROF testbed's capabilities, we developed a set of
educational modules focusing on robotic swarms, including the implementation of a
self-avoiding swarm in a constrained environment. Our testbed's design aims to
facilitate educational initiatives and accelerate the research momentum on robotic
swarms. Additionally, we present the SyROF testbed as a valuable resource for introductory
robotics courses, hands-on workshops, and research projects. The SyROF testbed can
be freely accessed through the open-source software repository located at https://syrof.github.io/. 
A detailed video presentation detailing the SyROF testbed is available at https://youtu.be/UiZ15eZ9XQ4. The current SyROF testbed is implemented using the following technologies: the Robot Operating System (ROS 2) for the underlying robot control framework, specifically the Colonial Agent world  for mobile robot simulation, paired with a new, high-level SyROF testbed abstraction implemented in the Java programming language. Testbed users can implement robotic swarms using the provided SyROF testbed environment and execute the resulting programs on various robot platforms, such as the Roomba, the Turtlebot, or the ZIMI robot, all of which are readily compatible with the SyROF testbed. To expedite the research and educational process, we have further optimized the testbed environment to automatically install the required dependencies, streamlining program development, verification, and execution on the chosen robotic platform. The SyROF testbed is designed to address several challenges typically encountered in robotic swarm development, with transparent synchronization, real-world application relevance, and the incorporation of the Timed Input/Output Automata (TIOA) programming paradigm being three key contributing factors. Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable effort,
so many researchers opt for pre-training their model on a different task before
further refining it using a smaller annotated dataset.  A commonly used method
for pre-training involves instructing a model to identify object categories in
images without the need for labels. However, this approach often yields mixed
results for segmentation of unmarked objects.  A novel approach for pre-training
involves educating a model how to accurately estimate depth dimensions from
unmarked images.  Our study provides numerical proof that depth estimation can
be successfully applied to unmarked videos, and that using depth estimates can
significantly boost performance when training a model on smaller, label-based
datasets.  Our depth estimation model has also been applied to a widely known
benchmark for evaluating self-driving vehicle technology, producing competitive
results when combined with other features.  The study's findings demonstrate that
using depth estimates can be a practical and efficient alternative to using
categorical data for pre-training a model.  The source code for the model has
been made available for public access at https://github.com/alex-righi/deeptown7. 
This study was supported by FAPEMIG and by Toyota Motor Corporation.

The susceptibility of facial recognition systems to fraudulent presentations restricts their adoption in high-stakes applications. Effective countermeasures against these deceptive attempts are vital for the safe integration of facial recognition technology. Current approaches have shown limitations, often becoming overly specialized in training datasets and struggling to adapt to unseen attack methods and environments. In this research, transfer learning is applied from the vision transformer model to tackle the challenge of detecting unknown anti-spoofing attacks. Experimental results conducted on widely accessible datasets showcase the feasibility of using transfer learning, achieving better generalization across domains with the ViT architecture, and performing competitively against state-of-the-art approaches on the CASIA-FASD dataset, and more effectively handles attacks not present in the training dataset. Moreover, our model surpasses existing solutions in the US3E dataset with a substantial increase in accuracy. The code and settings used in this study are freely available on the GitHub repository, https://github.com/ORZ-EE/computervision12. Our model has been designated as oracle_net in the repository.

Deep reinforcement learning stands out as a promising AI paradigm for instructing machines via environmental interaction and adaptive learning from their errors. Despite initial expectations, however, its successful application in the automotive industry remains elusive. Following in the footsteps of notable achievements by Google DeepMind in mastering Atari games and Go, we have developed a comprehensive framework for autonomous driving that leverages deep reinforcement learning. Given the complexity and variability of driving tasks, which can't be adequately modeled via traditional methods, this approach represents an important step forward. In this paper, we provide a detailed overview of the driving challenge as a suitable environment for large-scale simulation-based learning, outline the core learning problems and how they can be addressed, and provide an in-depth explanation of our proposed driving framework. Our framework's initial results demonstrate its ability to learn crucial driving skills, such as controlled starting and maneuvering in the environment. These accomplishments validate the potential of deep reinforcement learning to deliver safe and capable autonomous driving performances. Furthermore, they lay the groundwork for the essential research questions and challenges that must be addressed in this area. In the end, we predict that the application of safe autonomous driving will become a substantial real-world demonstration of the deep reinforcement learning technology.
