Through the National Quantum Initiative and Department of Energy's support, our work at the Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center at Fermilab aims to create a 2-meter diameter by approximately 1.5-meter tall experimental space capable of achieving extremely low millikelvin temperatures using a novel cryogenic platform. 
This cutting-edge cryogenic platform, founded on superconducting radiofrequency technology typically used in accelerator cavities, is designed to support three-dimensional superconducting qubit structures. This document outlines the baseline specifications and key features of the newly conceived platform. Furthermore, a companion document will detail the detailed design and the results of a demonstration prototype. Here, we will detail the design choices and requirements of the platform's footprint. Firstly, we will examine the platform's scientific objectives and constraints, followed by an explanation of the platform's design and lastly, a discussion of the platform's prospective scientific contributions. In this platform's base implementation, we will explore the integration of multiple features such as 3D superconducting qubit structures, 3He refrigeration, RF technology, magnetic field applications and pick-up coil technologies. Ultimately, this platform has the potential to significantly expand the scope of cryogenic applications in quantum computing. This led to the investigation of whether the trend holds true for real-world Python applications. By creating a static analysis tool, researchers examined a large sample of popular Python projects and MicroPython projects, comparing their findings to previous studies. The analysis showed that a substantial proportion of Python projects exhibit at least one crypto API misuse. The good design of some Python crypto libraries appears to significantly reduce the likelihood of misuses compared to studies involving Java and C. The results suggest a beneficial impact of sound API design on reducing crypto-related security risks in Python applications. The ultimate goal is to ensure secure data exchange between clients and servers, achieving a security gap of less than 4% - a figure comparable to the latest study on Java. BMOA_p is a part of the family of F(p,q,s) spaces introduced by R. Zhao and serves as the M\"{o}bius invariant subspaces of the Dirichlet spaces D^p_{p-1}. Our focus lies in analyzing the maximal subspace of strong continuity for semigroups of operators, exploring sufficient and necessary conditions on the infinitesimal generator of phi for the semigroup [phi_t, BMOA_p] to equal VMOA_p. We also establish the connection between the maximal subspace of strong continuity and the Volterra-type operators T_g, specifically examining which symbols g make T_g bounded or compact from BMOA to BMOA_1, while also investigating the relationship between compactness and weak compactness of T_g on BMOA_p when 1 < p < 2. Furthermore, our findings regarding the compactness of T_g on BMOA_p allow us to answer a question posed by C. Cowen and S. MacPederson regarding the compactness of T_g on BMOA. Additionally, our analysis yields conditions on the generation parameters alpha and beta which ensure the compactness or weak compactness of the shift operator T on BMOA_{p} or VMOA_p. Our findings also provide an affirmative answer to a question posed by J. Xiao regarding the weak compactness of T on VMOA. Finally, our research establishes the connection between our results on the shift operator T on BMOA_{p} or VMOA_p and a model problem in the theory of integral operators of Baxter. Our study corresponds to the case where 1 < p < 2. It appears that sufficient conditions for the compactness of T_g on BMOA_p when 1 < p < 2 are precise, while these conditions are broader for the case where p > 2. Thus, the case of p = 1 seems to be the most challenging among the three. Therefore, the case of p = 1 is studied separately in the second part of this dissertation. Understanding universal properties of a critical quantum spin chain model requires identifying key components of conformal field theory, notably the coefficients of operator product expansion, which describe operator fusion. Research suggests that these coefficients can be computed using wavefunction overlaps of low-energy states in the spin chain. We have demonstrated that central charge, conformal dimensions, and operator product expansion coefficients are encoded in wavefunction overlaps, accompanied by universal corrections that rely on cyclic orbifold CFT content. This approach allows for numerical computation of all conformal data solely based on low-energy eigenstates, a method that was verified in the Ising and XXZ models. Additionally, we used this method to study the Haagerup model and determined the central charge and lowest scaling dimension of a specific spin-1 operator. We also observed systematic deviations between our numerical results and theoretical values, which we attributed to universal corrections, thereby validating the CFT state reconstruction approach. This method may also contribute to the study of critical quantum spin chain models with additional symmetries. The study further sheds light on the broader implications of the principle of boundary matching, a concept from two-dimensional critical CFT, in the context of one-dimensional models. All numerical computations were conducted using the density matrix Monte Carlo method. Moreover, we propose a deeper connection between CFT data and the generalized Cassion's relation, which concerns the density of states in the spin chain model. Last but not least, we also uncovered indications of spin-1 operator scaling dimensions through a more conventional approach to CFT data reconstruction. The findings of this study lay the groundwork for future numerical investigations of critical quantum spin chain models using the method of CFT state reconstruction. Such research may also create new pathways for analyzing more complex systems. Two possible extensions of the work have also been suggested, first one involving the application of massless scalar field to CFT data reconstruction and second one involving the case of boundary-tractable models. Using the method of CFT state reconstruction in the spin chain allowed for a study of the scaling behavior of eigenstates, which showed that in the long rod limit, a scaling model emerges, characterized by a specific set of universal excitations. We have also computed scaling dimensions and level densities of spin excitations in the Ising and XXZ models. Moreover, we obtained precise finite-size corrections to critical exponents in the Ising and XXZ models. Automated part-of-speech (POS) annotation is a crucial task for linguistics and natural language processing, typically addressed through machine learning. Although the problem is largely solved for contemporary languages, historical corpora pose significant challenges, primarily due to limited native speaker interaction and a lack of training data. Compounding this issue, historical texts lack standardized sentence structures and orthographies, making automated POS tagging more complex and error-prone. In light of these complexities, instead of assigning single tags with uncertainty, POS tagging algorithms should allow for probabilistic outcomes. We propose applying the concept of set-valued prediction, enabling POS taggers to suggest a set of potential tags rather than guessing a single one. The objective is to strike a balance between ensuring a high likelihood of the correct tag being included while minimizing the number of suggested candidates. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating set-valued prediction leads to improved performance compared to single-value approaches. The proposed method is particularly beneficial for applications involving historical languages. The source code is publicly accessible via the GitHub repository https://github.com/jasmekusz/historical-pos-tagging. The research was funded by a grant from the National Research Agency of France (ANR), reference number PROJ-2018-1-ARX-17-03. This study was carried out in collaboration with the Universite de Lille, the Centre de Recherche en Histoire et Civilisation, and the Bibliothque Nationale de France. The data used in this research are part of the ArchiText project, implemented by the IN2S2 Platform of the Universite de Lille. The platform operates under the responsibility of the President of the French Republic. The research involved collecting and annotating a corpus of 18,522 sentences from the 16th to the 19th centuries, which was trained using the Renaissance language model. The curriculum was established through a combination of cross-sectional and longitudinal approaches. The training data consisted of the French Bible, the works of Michel de Montaigne, and the writings of Voltaire. The evaluation was conducted using two test corpora from the Bibliothque Nationale de France. The goal is to ultimately create a tagged corpus of the French language from the Middle Ages to the present. The research is part of the special collection of the Bibliothque Nationale de France. The findings demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, and future directions include exploring the use of neural networks for POS tagging. This research focuses on developing a method to calculate a utility function from a non-differentiable but locally Lipschitz candidate of a demand function. Using this method, we derive two new criteria that a demand function candidate must meet. First, it must be symmetrical and have a negatively semi-definite Slutsky matrix, and second, it must be a concave function. Utilizing recent results on the existence of a solution to a specific non-differentiable convex programming problem, we prove that a demand function candidate can be converted to a valid utility function within a specified Fejer sequence. This approach is then demonstrated in a numerical experiment. Additionally, the challenges of working with a non-differentiable but locally Lipschitz candidate of a demand function emerge, particularly in the need to employ a variety of approximation techniques, such as numerical integration and polynomial approximation. This approach is also illustrated in the numerical experiment described later in the paper. With an increasing number of applications where a demand function may need to be non-differentiable, we believe that developing new and efficient algorithms for calculating a valid utility function from a demand function candidate will become a crucial area of research in the field of economic theory. As an example of such an application, we note that the model developed by Gayle and Miller (2020) provides strong evidence that a farmer's cost function may exhibit a locally Lipschitz property. Therefore, developing a non-differentiable but locally Lipschitz demand function candidate from a cost function is also an important research direction, particularly in the context of competitive equilibrium. Using numerical experiments, we find that our algorithm can effectively calculate a valid utility function from a demand function candidate within a reasonably short time frame. This is particularly evident in the need to establish a relationship between a demand function candidate and a utility function, which may not be unique. Our research presents an innovative technique for accelerating variational quantum algorithms based on hidden inverse methods to counter coherent errors. By incorporating inverse gate implementations, noise levels are diminished and the robustness of the quantum circuit improves. This strategy proves particularly effective in multiple error scenarios, particularly where the noise factor and the gate's inverse have an inverse relationship. We successfully integrated this noise-mitigation approach within a variational quantum eigensolver running on a superconducting quantum processor to find the ground-state energy of the hydrogen molecule, and observed substantial energy fluctuations reductions during the parameter learning process in the VQE algorithm. This advancement resulted in the reduction of necessary iterations to reach a stable value. In addition to hardware experimentation, our findings include comprehensive analysis through error-sensitivity assessment in realistic noisy quantum channels. The hidden inverse method was found to deliver substantial performance gains over current noise-mitigation techniques in certain scenarios, and its adaptability makes it suitable for present and expected quantum processing units. Since this method is entirely gate-based, it can be seamlessly incorporated into future quantum algorithms for potential speedup. Furthermore, our study examines the degree to which coherent error influence on the inverse gate affects the circuit's resilience, and discusses the trade-off between hardware resources and circuit robustity. Based on our investigation involving multiple molecule systems, the most effective noise-mitigation strategy is a combination of inverse methods and classical optimization techniques. Overall, our research highlights the hidden inverse method's vast potential as a versatile and robust noise-mitigation approach suitable for practical quantum computing applications. The source code for implementing the method is freely accessible at https://github.com/QualityMechanics/Research-hiq-VAE. 

This paper is an expanded version of our previous communication in ArXiv, with fresh discussions added, particularly on the degree to which coherent error affects the inverse gate effectively to counter noise. We have further emphasized the general applicability of the noise-mitigation strategy in various quantum computing systems. The study is meant to contribute knowledge in the field and attract the interest of researchers working on practical quantum computing algorithms. The source code for implementing the method has been provided for reproducibility purposes, and is freely accessible at https://github.com/QualityMechanics/Research-hiq-VAE.

We develop a systematic method to study the impact of mass on the pole mass in QCD using heavy quark flavors, specifically for the top quark, through multiple iterations of RG evolution with higher-order mass terms, considering all possible outcomes in the mass matrix, thereby quantifying the pole mass's ambiguity to be less than 300 MeV, including higher-order contributions. This method may be further expanded to analyze the pole mass of the bottom quark and is exclusively applicable to heavy quark flavors. Furthermore, utilizing an approximation technique, the systematic pole mass RG evolution is carried out with the pole mass itself, achieving one-loop accuracy over multiple stages. This approach is then employed to analyze systematic mass-and-flavor-violating effects in the c-to-b transition and the top quark's mass splitting from its lightest state. Although this research is primarily driven by precision computations for the top quark and mixed QCD-flavour problems, it also faces challenges associated with significant numerical uncertainty in the process. This numerical uncertainty stems from several convergent series in the process, including those used to compute the top quark mass, which are known as the QCD-dispersed series. An alternative representation of this series, based on QCD-fundamental parameters, is suggested as a means to alleviate this issue. Moreover, a new method to compute these series has been developed using systematic beta-functions and characteristic scales. This approach also holds potential for applications in the analysis of quantum mechanical potential corrections for very-heavy quark potentials and vice versa. Additionally, a new method to compute the harmonic series, relevant in the process, has been developed using systematic beta-functions and characteristic scales. The associated reproducing kernels for Bergman spaces with p = q = 2 and α > 1 are also analyzed, yielding interesting observations. Furthermore, specific examples are examined to determine the tightness of these estimates. While the p = q = 2 scenario offers clarity, with tightness established in this case, uncertainty remains for other cases. Our findings draw from both recent and previously established studies, ultimately culminating in a complete understanding of hypercontractive inequalities in the p = 2 context. Specifically, we note that: 
  * When α > 1, the inequality holds with tightness in the scenario where p < q.
  * When α > 1, the inequality holds with tightness in the scenario where p > q.
  * When α < 1, the inequality holds with tightness in the scenario where p < q.
  * When α < 1, the inequality holds with tightness in the scenario where p > q. 
In general cases, where 0 < p < q < 2 or q > p > 0, the inequality remains valid but its tightness remains a topic of investigation. cost. Our research focuses on developing an intelligent system for diagnosing
COVID-19 using low-dose and ultra-low-dose CT scans that are both safe and more
cost-effective. We integrated a 3D-U-Net-based neural network with a spatial
self-attention mechanism to enhance our diagnostic accuracy. Utilizing data from
the COVID19-Chest-MRI dataset, which incorporates multi-channel images, and the

system over traditional classification methods. Our innovative solution
accomplished an impressive accuracy rating of 95%, surpassing the industry
standard by 10%. In real-world clinical settings, our method outperformed other
models, including a transformer encoder, while using the fewest number of
parameters. As a result, our system offers the highest possible balance of
diagnostic accuracy and efficiency. By addressing the challenges associated with
limited data sets, our research provides insights into overcoming industry hurdles.

To generate top-quality quadrilateral meshes on complex computer-aided design (CAD) models efficiently, we propose an integrated solution. A versatile mesh with numerous irregular points is initially created, which allows for extensive local modifications. Subsequently, the mesh topology and coordinates are optimized using efficient algorithms derived from established frameworks. Notably, our method enables the construction of high-order meshes that are suitable for computational analysis with ease. We evaluate our approach by comparing its performance against state-of-the-art quadrilateral mesh generation methods, which demonstrates its superiority in terms of producing more optimal meshes through various numerical benchmarks. Additionally, our technique is made available as an open-source library to facilitate mesh refinement in visualizations and computational simulations. It is accessible at: \url{https://pyrefine-open-source.github.io/Refine/}. Moreover, a user demonstration interactive session is hosted at: \url{https://pyrefine-open-source.github.io/refineinteractive}.

Pearson's correlation coefficient is frequently employed as a measure of association. In cases where the relationships are not linear, more complex techniques like partial correlation analysis, which accounts for the effects of relevant variables, is considered a more suitable approach. Existing partial correlation estimators are often prone to significant errors in non-linear scenarios. This research introduces a novel partial correlation function based on conditional chi-square distances in Gaussian mixtures, which has the advantage of providing invariant results with respect to the distribution of the input data. Simulation experiments demonstrate that this estimator performs exceptionally well even in non-Gaussian cases, and its accuracy surpasses that of the standard partial correlation estimator in certain non-linear scenarios. The proposed method is further validated through the analysis of real-world data sets. In particular, this research involves investigating the relationship between EEG signals and an individual's mental state as an example of explaining a variable by one or more others. The study involved varying numbers of Gaussian components in the mixture model to accommodate non-Gaussian data, which was responsible for significant improvements in the accuracy of the estimated partial correlation coefficient. The obtained results suggest a very strong linear association between the mentioned EEG bands and states of mind, which correlates with existing knowledge on the topic. The proposed estimator has significant theoretical implications, offering new avenues for understanding the association between variables that cannot be described using linear models. This research is a crucial stepping stone for exploring non-linear partial correlations, which could lead to the development of more sophisticated machine learning algorithms in the future. The proposed method has been implemented in a publicly available R package called Accrpt. The majority of the paper's content, except for Section 7, is relevant to readers without a background in machine learning. We investigate the two- or three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations defined within a bounded region. This model takes into account an external force that introduces instability and is constrained by a boundary within the specified area. The goal of our work is to provide a detailed analysis of the Cauchy problem for this model, focusing on whether the solution results in smooth motion or if it develops singularities over a specific, possible shorter time period. In the case of a two-dimensional system and certain conditions regarding the space where the solution is measured, we demonstrate that only smooth motion occurs. In the specific case where the system dimensions are three, we confirm a previously established finding and provide a more in-depth understanding of the local well-posedness of this model in a specific space. This work is a result of merging previously separate theories and is further supported by calculating explicit constants for a specific space. The resulting findings in this work have significant implications and help in understanding the behavior of the solutions when the time period extends indefinitely. Among these, post-hoc methods have been identified as the most practical solutions for intricate models that operate as "black-boxes." Recent studies have exposed limitations in local surrogate-based post-hoc explanations regarding their inherent reliability, especially in critical applications such as human-centric recommendation tasks. Moreover, an ideal explanation should enhance key aspects of user experience including clarity and trustworthiness, posing additional challenges to the current approaches. However, a novel, state-of-the-art post-hoc explanation method called LEAP has been proposed to address these issues effectively. Specifically, LEAP utilizes a hybrid approach combining logic and learning to create explanations that are more coherent, understandable, and ultimately, trustworthy. Through thorough experimentation, the superiors of LEAP have been demonstrated whencompared to other cutting-edge post-hoc methods, showcasing their capacity to provide reliable explanations. Furthermore, user evaluations have validated the effectiveness of LEAP in enhancing key aspects of user experience like transparency and trustworthiness. Lastly, practical case studies have been conducted to measure the impact of explaining recommended content on user perceived trust, showcasing LEAP's practical applications and explanations' ability to real-world deployment. As a whole, this research contributes to the development of trustworthy recommender systems, shedding light on the crucial role explaining-based interface plays in fostering user trust. Research has shown that certain distributional assumptions are required to guarantee the reliable learnability of complex concepts when evaluating a specific type of data. In response, researchers have developed several robust machine learning frameworks based on either the assumption of local uniformity or local ergodicity. However, the foundations of these frameworks rely on an unspecified subset of assumptions, which raises the need to clarify their individual importance. This research addresses a particular component of this issue by demonstrating that the existence of local ergodic membership queries is a crucial prerequisite for the reliable application of several established machine learning methods across various domains. This requirement is further reinforced by the creation of a universal framework that incorporates the query and its associated implications for the scope of learnable concepts within AAG datasets. Additionally, the existence of local ergodic queries also facilitates a broader distributional flexibility in the context of robust empirical risk minimization, providing more effective and reliable learning outcomes. To support these findings, the researchers provide formal proofs and illustrate the practical efficacy of this query in realistic scenarios, highlighting its potential to significantly improve the robustness of machine learning models when properly applied. They also provide examples that demonstrate the limitations of commonly used learning methods when local ergodic queries are not available. By expanding upon the traditional framework of distributionally robust learning, this research provides significant contributions to our understanding of this critical machine learning paradigm. First, the researchers demonstrate that the assumption of local ergodicity is a necessary component of several popular learning methods and datasets, including those based on Gal-Yam's criteria. This requirement is not met by the broader class of distributionally robust learning methods. Second, the researchers show that the existence of local ergodic queries has significant implications for the reliable application of empirical risk minimization. This research expands upon recent findings by Kanniah and Zaidi et al., who explored the connection between local uniformity and risk minimization. Our previous research significantly sped up Sinkhorn iteration by taking advantage of a kernel matrix's inherent properties, transforming its $O(N^2)$ complexity to $O(N)$ efficiency. This paper delves deeper into kernel matrix characteristics by defining and applying two key concepts, Lower-ColLinear Triangular Matrices and Upper-ColLinear Triangular Matrices. By showing that these matrices can perform scalar multiplication, transpose, and matrix multiplication in linear time, effectively acting as data structures, thus enhancing Sinkhorn iteration to a logarithmic complexity basis on the number of elements $N$. In addition, these matrix operations also facilitate efficient computation of their eigenvalues, trace, and reciprocal of the adjugate matrix, all in $O(N)$ complexity. We develop an innovative approach to describe the friction caused by radiation experienced by particles moving through a medium with mechanical resistance. We model this interaction as a scattering event involving a charged particle traversing a medium with surface properties. This description effectively captures the phenomenon where charged particles lose energy due to the medium they pass through, a phenomenon observed in materials but also in empty space with charged particles interacting with photons. We compare our new description to the standard synchrotron radiation formula and find that for particles undergoing geometric scattering, their radiation loss will be directly proportional to the energy of the particle and the logarithm of the particle's energy relative to its scattering angle. We also consider the effects of other scattering events, finding that for any given angle, there will be a threshold energy level beyond which the radiation loss will increase rapidly. We apply our new description to understand the feedback this may have on the dynamics of particle interactions and motion within the medium, a phenomenon that may be of importance in understanding cosmic particle behavior. Nuclear interactions may need to be accounted for as well, particularly in the case of very high-energy particles. We also investigate the potential to directly observe these radiation losses through particle experiments. Our new description may also be relevant to other fields, such as astrophysics research, to understand how particles may behave and interact within the universe. Our results are shown to be consistent with existing research on this topic, providing a more complete and accurate understanding of particle interactions and may be applied to other fields of physics to study the behavior of charged particles and their interactions with various media. Many complex systems feature networks where interactions between diverse agents combine simple local rules to create complex emergent behaviors. While recent research has found connections between network structure and the underlying dynamic processes, detecting random complex patterns remains a pressing challenge. We develop a new, straightforward method grounded in mathematical techniques to discover and manage complex patterns that arise on large-scale networks, even without prior knowledge of their structure. This approach identifies underlying dynamics by analyzing a collection of snapshots representing network states over time. By applying operator-theoretic methods, it converts complex patterns into a linear format, facilitating model predictive control. We show that our proposed method simplifies a complex problem typically difficult to solve in large networks, transforming it into a more tractable and efficient optimization problem with a reduced number of variables. Extensive tests demonstrate that this approach effectively extracts meaningful patterns that can be used for control, and that its solutions approximate those of the original complex problem while being much more practical for large-scale networks. Furthermore, we utilize this technique to uncover underlying patterns in real-world data sets and provide a tangible benefit by developing control policies that can be easily implemented. Overall, this research highlights that underlying network dynamics are key to uncovering complex patterns, and that our proposed method is a effective way to extract meaningful patterns that can be used for control, and that its solutions approximate those of the original complex problem while being much more practical for large-scale networks. Research has revealed that a liquid-solid interface attached to a solid boundary can move more easily than assumed, influencing the stability and evolution of liquid films. By taking into account this increased slip, our study examines how liquid drops evolve when placed under a unidirectional pressure, focusing on the film that forms on a cylindrical surface. We found that a small amount of slip can cause perturbations to grow faster, ultimately leading to the breakdown of axisymmetric film behavior and the emergence of sinusoidal fluctuations in the liquid film. In contrast, higher levels of slip lead to a more complex scenario in which these fluctuations can either disappear or remain unstable, causing the film to break up into droplets. Our research uses theoretical calculations to determine how liquid drops evolve based on the level of slip, ranging from smaller drops for low slip to a continuous process of film breakdown into droplets for higher slip. We also found that a critical pressure exists beyond which the film will always break up into droplets, influenced by the level of slip. For example, a relatively small overpressure of about 10% is sufficient to break up the film when there is moderate slip. The findings from our study have implications for the use of capsules in medical applications, providing valuable insights into how drugs or liquid components may be released from an encapsulated liquid. This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers. We explore a median-based output generation strategy, which offers advantages such as being more representative, robust to training data irregularities, and enabling incremental synthesis. This method is in line with a broader goal of concurrently modelling durations and acoustic features at a frame-level. Evaluations show that this approach performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods in predicting the median duration of unseen natural speech. Additionally, a comparison of this method with a mean-based approach reveals that median-based modelling yields more realistic sentence-level duration phrases in speech synthesis. Ultimately, this method demonstrates potential as a starting point for more efficient and accurate duration inference. This study undertakes a comprehensive analysis of existing datasets pertinent to the analysis of historical documents through image-based techniques. Specifically, this involves exploring collections of handwritten manuscripts and early printed materials. Acquiring suitable datasets for research on historical documents employing various machine learning methodologies necessitates identifying appropriate datasets. Unfortunately, selecting datasets from the diverse pool of data, varying in script, format, degradation level, label representation, evaluation processes, and benchmarks poses a significant challenge. To address this challenge, this research conducts a meta-analysis on available datasets. A thorough, systematic selection process was adopted, based on established criteria, to identify 65 studies from the relevant literature, focusing on practical applications of machine learning for historical documents. Studies were evaluated against specific, objective measures and included in the meta-analysis, if they met these criteria. This research review is further divided into seven sections, each focused on a distinct task associated with historical documents: feature extraction, classification, recognition, synthesis, geometric analysis, page organization, and quality assessment. A total of 168 papers were reviewed, including 105 new studies, which supplements the existing knowledge in this area. Due to the inherent elasticity in their design, industrial robots that lack advanced precision-enhancing technology are only marginally effective for machining tasks. Besides issues related to structure, temperature, and support bearings, one major factor behind elasticity is the backlash in the transmission systems. This study proposes a method for improving trajectory precision using supplementary sensors and a novel feedback control strategy in combination with a feed-forward approach based on flatness. For this purpose, a novel dynamic model is introduced that accurately describes a flexible robotic joint as a two-mass system with pose-dependent inertia, nonlinear friction, nonlinear elasticity, and backlash. A feed-forward controller is designed using the flatness-based method to optimize movement quality, and a supplementary feedback controller is implemented to counteract external disturbances, utilizing real-time automatic differentiation to ensure swift computation. Finally, the proposed algorithms are tested in simulated and real-world experiments using a KUKA Quantec KR300 Ultra SE. The results demonstrate that our approach can effectively reduce positional errors by up to 3.7mm in the path tracking application. This gain in accuracy means that without modifying the robot's structure, our approach can enhance its performance by up to 15%. This improvement in turn enables the robot to successfully perform an accurate pick-and-place task without any adjustments to its trajectory. The proposed feed-forward controller also enables the robot to precisely follow a complex curved path in the presence of significant disturbances. These outcomes validate the novel dynamic model and the proposed feed-forward and feedback control strategy for improving robotic movement quality. They also show that with the right approach, a standard industrial robot can match the precision of a precision industrial robot, at least in terms of movement accuracy. Finally, our approach has the potential to significantly enhance the robustness of robotic applications by enabling the robot to effectively counteract common sources of elasticity. To further maximize the effectiveness of this approach, it is feasible to integrate it with a robust control strategy to counteract unexpected real-world disturbances, or to use model predictive control to optimize movement quality under constraints. These potential enhancements are the subjects of ongoing research. The source code for the algorithms presented in this study is publicly available on the GitHub repository at the URL: https://github.com/jpforhan/treetracking. Additionally, the study's simulations and real-time experiments were carried out using FLIR ENISEF-1 and Quanser Motion Simulator HW-Driver cards, and were integrated with the Tecplot visualization software. The project as a whole involved substantial efforts in development, and the associated cards, software, and telemetry data used in this study

One widely accepted method for evaluating electronic integrals in complex molecules involves a modified version of Becke's partitioning scheme, originally designed for functions that decline rapidly over distance. Due to the intricate nature of electronic potential maps in polyatomic molecules, they cannot be accurately represented by the product of separate functions for each atom. Consequently, effective electronic integration relies on the interdependence of atomic potential maps. Our study demonstrates the efficiency of Becke's partitioning scheme in tackling these interdependent relationships. By utilizing a modified version of this method, which accounts for the interatomic nature of electronic potential maps, we achieve high precision in integral calculations, leading to a decrease in computational time from the previous method. Moreover, our newly derived integrals based on the modified partitioning scheme yield highly accurate energy estimates in quantum chemistry simulations. In particular, our integration method is especially suited for complex systems like graphene and peptide systems, where detailed atomic potential maps play a critical role. Overall, our results indicate that our integration approach is both precise and efficient, making it ideally tailored for the analysis of large systems with dependent atomic potential maps. With the rapid advancements in high-performance computing, methods like these could become increasingly important in the simulation of ever-more complex biological systems. Domain theory's powerdomains hold significant importance in the semantics of non-deterministic programming languages.  This paper extends powerdomains to directed spaces - a concept equivalent to T_0 monotone-determined spaces.  Powerdomain-like spaces (upper, lower, and convex powerspaces) of directed spaces are defined through free algebras, and their existence and structures are shown for any directed space.  Notably, these spaces have distinct structures compared to powerdomains of directed-complete partial orders with Scott topology and other previously-introduced powerspaces.  Relationships between these different powerdomains are examined, and directed-space powerdomains are compared to those of their directed-complete subcategory.  A new relation between domains is introduced as a generalization of the continuous functions' relation, and is shown to be relevant to the directed setting.  Finally, this paper establishes the equivalence of two different definitions of T_0 monotone-determined spaces: one based on domain equations and the other based on the dual definition of L-domains.  The paper concludes with a characterization of compact elements in the directed setting of T_0 spaces.  A separate appendix examines the dcpo subcategory of zonal spaces, and compares the powerdomains of its partial order extension to the powerdomains of the entire category.  The appendix further explores the relationship between the powerdomains of the subcategory and the powerdomains of the entire category in the case where the partial order is a Scott domain.  The appendix also contains a characterization of compact elements in the partial order setting of T_0 zonal spaces. Past and potential future Earth climate states have included extremely warm 'hothouse' environments with unknown characteristics. The scarcity of hothouse climates in existing climate simulations might be due to a perfect storm of negative feedbacks. However, our findings suggest a different perspective, driven by two distinct approaches. Firstly, we recognize that stable and unstable climate states may exhibit distinct characteristics, rather than being representative of the same continuous spectrum. Secondly, the behavior of 'hothouse' climates under reduced greenhouse effect still exhibits significant dampening, rather than complete elimination. Building on these premises, our analyses reveal two crucial consequences. Firstly, in 'hothouse' climates, the water cycle is significantly reduced, but when reinstated, it contributes to a substantial amplification of equatorial temperature gradients. Secondly, the resulting changes in 'hothouse' environments, featuring temperature gradients akin to modern tropical environments, could be more prone to instability than previously suspected, characterized by widespread presence of double-ITCZ patterns, multiple equatorial warm-spot configurations and internal climate variability associated with stratospheric winds. These findings significantly advance the research of hothouse climates by shedding light on underlying physical mechanisms, thus potentially revolutionizing our understanding of this critical aspect of climate science. The findings further suggest that geographic variations in surface temperature could increasingly become a key indicator of climate change familiarity in the distant future, particularly under heightened greenhouse effect conditions. Ultimately, our knowledge of hothouse climates may ultimately contribute to the development of more effective climate change mitigation and adaptation strategies. While significant uncertainties still exist regarding many aspects of hothouse environments, our work offers a critical first step in leveraging climate science to investigate these critical environmental systems. The findings presented in this research are based on a comprehensive review of climate model data, specifically CMIP6, and include a detailed discussion of the underlying scientific principles that govern hothouse environments. The research further sustains existing calls for further investigation into this critical aspect of climate science via enhanced simulations, observations and theoretical analysis. The findings presented in this research are critical to the broader climate science community, including those that study both past and future hothouse environments, through their alignment with existing research results and insights. The research presented in this article is essential to the critical understanding of hothouse environments and may inform certain elements of future research, including the potential for novel climate simulations and theoretical analyses. The findings regarding the significant presence of double-ITCZ patterns in hothouse environments are significant advances in the research of tropical climates and may inform existing research on this critical aspect

The application of deep neural networks in medical image classification has shown great promise due to their advanced image mapping capabilities. Despite this, current deep learning-based methods rely heavily on the quality of the training data, specifically the accuracy of the labels. Conventional recollection and re-labeling processes, though possible, are often impractical and can be costly. Furthermore, these methods are not feasible when working with large datasets, causing significant issues with noise and inaccuracies in the classification process, leading to a decrease in the model's performance. Our research proposes a noise reduction-based method to refine the labeling process in large-scale medical image classification tasks by using the spatial relationships between images to identify and correct labeling errors. This is achieved through a statistical analysis of the class labels and images, followed by the iterative correction of inaccurate labels, ultimately improving the model's robustness and its ability to achieve higher classification accuracy when validated using cross-validation and the synthetic noisy data from real-world datasets. The proposed method demonstrated its effectiveness on the IncNetNet backbone by increasing the model's classification accuracy by up to 4% and by as much as 11% for specific organ types, especially when dealing with noisy datasets containing high levels of imperfections. These improvements open up new avenues for the practical application of deep neural networks in medical imaging, especially in the classification of complex datasets. The proposed method has the potential for further extension to other deep learning-based tasks, such as segmentation, where accurate image labeling is crucial. Define the norm of a function as its maximum absolute value over $Q_n$. Let $\Pi_1\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)$ be the set of polynomials of degree at most one, i.e., linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$. An interpolation projector $P$ is introduced that maps functions from $C(Q_n)$ to linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$, using nodes within $Q_n$. When the number of nodes is an Hadamard number, a non-uniform node set can be constructed such that the interpolation projector $P$, satisfying certain conditions, minimizes the norm. However, this minimization is not limited to norm $l_2$ but equally applicable to any other norm, e.g., $l_\infty$. Furthermore, it can be observed that the norm of the interpolation projector's error is not greater than the norm of the function itself in $l_\infty$, offering corollaries related to various norms, e.g., $l_2$. These findings extend previous results from interpolation theory to any norm, $l_p$. Moreover, an equidistant node set can be constructed over an $n$-dimensional torus, $T^n$, with period $2\pi$, and an interpolation projector's error has been estimated for the Lebesgue spaces, e.g., $L_2(Q_n)$. However, the Trigonal inequality provides a sharper bound than the one offered by the Immermann-Krylov inequality. In a total functions logic such as HOL, certain non-terminating functions are difficult to define directly. To overcome this limitation, a clock mechanism is often introduced to enforce termination after a specified evaluation depth. While commonly regarded as cumbersome, we argue that alternative methods of adding a clock exist, with varying levels of intrusion. We present a new approach that simplifies termination proofs without overly utilizing the clock mechanism, particularly illustrated through the context of functional big-step semantics for programming language interpretations. This method is further validated by applying it to the formalization of small-step semantics. Ultimately, we discovered that, in most cases, small-step and big-step semantics yield equivalent definitions, resulting in simplified termination proofs. These findings not only enhance HOL-like logic usability but also contribute to improved understandability of functional programming language semantics by highlighting the redundancy in certain termination proofs. To that end, we provide practical guidance on useful clock mechanisms usage. Moreover, the developed formalization of small-step semantics in HOL offers valuable insights, making it suitable for replication in similar formalization efforts. Utilizing first-principles calculations, our research involves analyzing silicene in relation to hexagonal boron nitride substrates. Silicene's behavior varies based on the thickness of the substrate, ranging from an insulating substrate to a metallic substrate. In the middle range of the substrate thickness, we found silicene to exhibit both insulating and metallic properties. However, upon further investigation, we discovered the insulating properties are due to hexagonal boron nitride's thickness, while the metallic properties are a result of interactions with the substrate. Notably, silicene's bandgap can be significantly increased by up to 5 eV through the incorporation of a monolayer of hexagonal boron nitride, making it suitable for various applications. Moreover, the bandgap can be controlled by adjusting the substrate thickness, providing the potential for silicene to be used in the development of innovative thermoelectric devices. The unique bandgap of silicene, coupled with its mechanical and electrical properties, allows it to be used in the optimization of metal-silicene bonds, ultimately leading to the potential for innovative applications in the fabrication of full nanoscale devices. The possibility of achieving room temperature integration of silicene is also within reach due to its remarkable temperature stability. In conclusion, the unique bandgap of silicene, combined with its exceptional nanoscale interaction capabilities and thermal stability, makes it an attractive choice for nanoelect mechanical switch development. Furthermore, our research identifies hexagonal boron nitride as an efficient insulating layer to be used in the integration of silicene, in contrast to metallic substrates. The exceptional mechanical and electrical properties of silicene also make it an attractive choice for the optimization of interactions with other materials. In addition, the thermal stability of silicene, coupled with its advanced nanoscale interaction capabilities, allows it to be used in the integration of other nanomaterials, such as graphene. In conclusion, the integration of silicene and graphene using hexagonal boric acid may hold the potential for the development of innovative nanoelect mechanical devices. The Sgr A East supernova remnant, located near the center of the Milky Way, has been examined using the 20 cm radio frequency interference (RFI) data collected by the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope. A novel RFI removal technique was applied to the RFI data contaminated Sgr A East image, utilizing the sparse representation and dictionary-based approach. Consequently, the RFI removal process enhanced the visibility of Sgr A East's features, thereby facilitating an assessment of its spectral characteristics. Based on the clean images and spectra produced by the method, it is estimated that Sgr A East is approximately 40,000 to 60,000 years old. Furthermore, by analyzing the synchrotron fill levels at 20 cm and 11 cm, it was found that Sgr A East's fill levels exhibit a positive correlation with surrounding ambient densities. A comparison with X-ray data has also revealed that Sgr A East exhibits X-ray-to-21 cm flux ratio values that align with typical supernova remnant parameters. Lastly, it is suggested that Sgr A East may be interacting with nearby molecular clouds, specifically G0.05+0.07, due to observed distortions in the eastern edge of the remnant. Utilizing Google Scholar's API to obtain daily COVID-19 related Google Trends data and national mortality rates, we applied various statistical methods, including cross-correlation, to explore relationships between news coverage and death rates. We develop a novel, yet efficient, method for augmenting existing data to enhance the learning capacity of reinforcement and imitation learning from experienced models. The policy generator network creates synthetic experiences based on the primary dataset, and a validator ensures these synthetic states have similar value functions to the original training data, thereby maintaining the validity of the learned model. Furthermore, the method can also be adapted to enhance robustness by creating states under various corruption scenarios and training a model to mimic the behavior of an expert model trained on these synthetic states. The proposed framework is versatile and can be incorporated into existing training procedures, including Q-learning, actor-critic methods, and generative adversarial networks, without requiring experience replay or curriculum learning. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method in several benchmark tasks, showcasing its potential to increase sample efficiency, particularly in challenging scenarios with limited or noisy expert data. Atomic magnetometers that utilize self-oscillating technology and driven by resonant modulation demonstrate enhanced sensitivity and dynamic range capabilities.
This technology, in conjunction with phase-coherent feedback from detected signals to modulation, enables the creation of a resonant spin maser system highly sensitive to changes in background magnetic fields.
Our system incorporates digital signal processing integrated into the maser feedback loop, thereby meeting the necessary phase condition for resonant precession.
Using a compact laser and mass-produced caesium vapour cell, it functions effectively in a 50 microtesla field and has the potential to be applied in portable geophysical magnetic field measurements.
Our results show a Cramer-Rao limited resolution of 50 fT at 1 second sampling rate and a 10 kHz bandwidth, indicating a suitable resolution for precise measurements.

For K3 surfaces with an automorphism having a Siegel disk, the associated Picard number falls between $0$ and $18$ and must be an even integer. Conversely, applying the technique of hypergeometric groups, K3 surface automorphisms possessing Siegel disks can be constructed to demonstrate all conceivable Picard numbers through the identification and computation of relevant algebraic numbers derived from Lefschetz-type formulas and their corresponding residues. Moreover, these automorphisms can be further detailed with explicit mappings and polynomial expressions representing their dynamics. Notably, for the scenario of a trivial Picard number, the associated automorphisms fall into the class of Araki-Yoshida inversions, whereas for the scenario of the maximum Picard number of $22$, the associated automorphisms can be shown to be finitely cyclic. Ultimately, in almost all cases, the dynamics of these K3 surface automorphisms can be represented by the hypergeometric function $_2F_1(1, 1; 2)$ and, in a few special instances, by the function $_3F_2(1, 1; 1, 2)$. Moreover, for the scenario of the maximum Picard number of $22$, the associated superperiods involve the resolution of $G_2$-linear Gauss-Manin connection, whose corresponding Argyres' family of rank-one polarized abelian surfaces can be identified and analyzed. Lastly, in a brief concluding segment, the issues related to the non- existence of finite cyclic Araki-Yoshida involutions for K3 surfaces will be addressed along with potential generalizations to higher types of varieties, particularly hyperk\"ahler varieties. Further specific mathematical insights will also be provided in two appendices, specifically addressing the relations between the derivatives of the Lefschetz type formulas and the resolutions of the associated linear problems, particularly for the scenario of the maximum Picard number of $22$. We introduce an extension to the MSSM/SUGRA model, where the transformation properties of certain scalars with respect to $SU(3)_H$ are analogous to those in the hidden sector and where these scalars acquire significant masses through their D-terms. The framework contains a neutralino ground state that is stable from the cosmological standpoint. The accompanying calculation of the relic density demonstrates that, in the (semi)hidden sector scenario, a pure bino neutralino can naturally obtain the correct relic density, whereas this is challenging in the conventional SUGRA framework. Our approach to training a neural network to identify hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali is outlined in this work. We investigate the viability of leveraging transfer learning for these languages due to their shared origin, which lends them a degree of similarity. Our experiment's implementation on low-powered hardware yields results that hold up against those of more costly models, a phenomenon we also demonstrate with language models. Additionally, our project's source code and model weights are publicly accessible, which could facilitate future research. We suggest that limited data sets and language similarity may facilitate the development of reliable hate-speech detection tools for languages with limited available data. We propose that efficient computing hardware, such as Google's Edge TPUs, is crucial for this endeavor. We also address the ethical considerations of working with data that is potentially hateful or offensive. We advocate for transparency regarding the processing of such data and the implementation of measures to prevent its propagation. Our approach to handling potentially offensive data is presented as an example. In nuclear and particle physics, being able to identify the direction of nuclear recoils is a significant advantage. This capability, achievable at low energies, could help verify the existence of dark matter, examine dark matter events, and gather data on neutrino interactions. Operating since 2014, the NEWSdm experiment in Italy utilizes liquid xenon and has produced substantial advancements in low-recoil energy detection. By employing an array of four photodetectors, each with a large viewing angle around the focal point, this experiment can determine the direction of nuclear recoils. Following a significant improvement to increase sensitivity, a detection system with wider viewing angles was tested. This system, characterized by wider fields of view, has been incorporated into the experiment, and the current results and future objectives will be discussed. Moreover, a new sub-detection system, named NEWSarm, has been developed with adjustable arms capable of rotating around the focal point. This enhancement has been detailed, along with plans to integrate this detector into the primary experiment for an upgraded version of the NEWSdm. Finally, a multi-disciplinary concept involving neural networks and Monte Carlo simulations was developed to create an artificial neural network, which was trained on realistic data of both background and dark matter signals. This concept could potentially be applied to the analysis of the upgraded experiment's findings.

A comprehensive analysis of commercial driving behavior requires considering various personal characteristics and environmental influences like weather and road conditions. Current driver-assessment systems, relying solely on behavior data, may yield unfair and inaccurate results by neglecting contextual factors. To rectify this issue, we introduce a new assessment method called Expert-centered Driver Assessment. By incorporating expert input from multiple stakeholders in the industry, our approach ensures that the decision-making process is informed by the nuanced interplay between behaviors and environmental conditions. Based on a literature review and expert consultation, we identified crucial factors impacting driving behavior and designed an uncertainty-reflective questionnaire format to capture experts' diverse views. Fuzzy set modeling enabled us to incorporate these uncertainties into our analysis. The proposed Expert-centered Driver Assessment method is characterized by high accuracy, fairness, and transparency, and it consistently reflects the stakeholders' viewpoints. Our study also demonstrates how to address complexity and ambiguity in various assessment objectives. By leveraging these strengths, our expert-centered approach can be applied to various driver-assessment scenarios. Moreover, our methodology may be adapted for use in other fields where dealing with multiple stakeholders and contextual factors is critical. Additionally, our analysis may serve as a foundation for further investigations into fair and accurate assessment methods in industry applications. By considering the viewpoints of experts, our approach may serve as a potential solution to the reverse engineering problem in industry contexts. Our expert-centered approach is comprised of four core sub-tasks: selecting assessment objectives and relevant stakeholders, designing questionnaire formats, combining expert inputs, and interpreting overall results. We utilized these sub-tasks to incorporate contextual factors into our analysis, which resulted in our expert-centered approach outperforming current state-of-the-art methods in several key aspects. By comparing our approach with intelligence-driven assessment methods, our results illustrate the importance of considering contextual information as well as incorporating multiple stakeholders' viewpoints in the decision-making process. To validate our approach empirically, an actual driver-assessment system utilizing our expert-centered methodology has been successfully implemented within the industry. By comparing our proposed methodology with existing intelligence-driven approaches, our results from real-world applications confirm that our expert-centered approach achieves high accuracy, fairness, and transparency in the assessment process. Our findings also ascribe our expertise a high level of credibility within this context. By leveraging our expert-centered approach, our analysis reveals several actionable insights that may aid in improving road safety and driving behavior through personalized advice. By comparing our proposed methodology with intelligence-driven approaches, our results from real-world applications verify the effectiveness of our expert-centered approach and shed light on its potential to address challenges in industry

This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was used, comprising unseen scene text instances not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic text recognition task and a focused word recognition task.
The proposed COMA approach demonstrated a word-recognition rate of 64.71% on the validation set.
The competition showed that existing OCR models still require significant improvement for accurately reading novel, unseen text instances.

In our research, we conduct experiments on Rayleigh-Taylor Instability by introducing a controlled disturbance through magnetic levitation technology. We perform identical experiments under both normal and microgravity settings, yielding remarkable results: identical setups produce identical outcomes, a consequence of which is that the displacement of density interfaces can be accurately predicted using a combination of quadratic equations. The underlying cause of this phenomenon is a fundamental symmetry in fluid dynamics that arises from Hamilton's Principle. The application of this symmetry to our specific study is facilitated by a Lagrangian approach, which demonstrates that microgravity simplifies the analysis by reducing the problem to a fundamental geometric challenge involving one-dimensional surfaces. The significance of our research lies in its use of modern tools to re-examine classical problems, producing novel insights and perspectives. Ultimately, our study not only provides an in-depth explanation of RTI but also showcases the elegance of Hamiltonian mechanics in action. The Sinkhorn algorithm remains a widely-used solution to the Schrödinger problem. While it's well-documented that this algorithm converges when a solution exists, a linear convergence rate is achieved only if a pre-defined regularization parameter is optimal. The regularizer's optimal value relies on the solution itself, necessitating an additional estimate. In this work, a modified algorithm is introduced that overcomes this challenge, ensuring convergence at a linear rate without relying on the optimal regularization parameter, and it remains applicable for both continuous and discrete cases. The article also examines the scenarios in which this modified algorithm avoids getting stuck in suboptimal solutions. Theoretical analyses suggest that this modified algorithm performs better than its classical counterpart when attempting to approximate an unattainable solution, while achieving a higher likelihood of reaching the global optimum with fewer iterations. To validate these claims, the algorithm's performance is compared with the original Sinkhorn algorithm in a few relevant use cases. The open-source implementation of this modified algorithm can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/Anguier/NormalizedDLIKE. To analyze the center-of-mass motion of hundreds of ${}^{171}$Yb ions arranged in a two-dimensional Wigner crystal, we utilize the density matrix approach. In our study, the behavior of an individual ion within this array is examined under the influence of both nearest-neighbor Coulomb interactions and laser cooling. By investigating spin dephasing, caused by uneven laser power among ions, we discover that a decrease in the lateral confinement leads to enhanced Coulomb interactions and, consequently, accelerated spin dephasing. Conversely, increasing the plane of motion has an inverse effect on this phenomenon. Furthermore, our findings indicate that a temperature gradient within the array can greatly prolong the time required to reach equilibrium in the center-of-mass motion. In an effort to minimize this effect, we suggest supplementing the array with a few-motion degrees of freedom. To implement this, we demonstrate the process of splitting a linear trap into two distinct modes, and the subsequent transfer of ions from a linear trap to a planar motional state via a rapid switch of the magnetic gradient gauge field. In our experimental setup, the success of this process is verified through the detection of the crystal's rotation period via image analysis of fluorescence. Ultimately, our research provides the framework for optimizing the center-of-mass motion of large ion arrays and may find applications in future quantum simulation protocols. In doing so, we identify optimal conditions for minimizing the influence of Coulomb interactions on the center-of-mass motion and facilitate the implementation of innovative algorithms aimed at leveraging ion interactions to speed up computations. Moreover, our research into a few-motion degree-of-freedom demonstrates the feasibility of employing tailored laser cooling to enable the center-of-mass cooling of large ion arrays, thereby paving the way for future large-scale ion cameras capable of detecting nanometer-scale objects. In particular, the use of a large ion array in which the crystal rotation period can be manipulated may enable the detection and identification of individual rotation photons produced during the laser cooling process, thereby facilitating the imaging of static as well as moving nanometer-scale objects. In conclusion, our research explores the feasibility of utilizing large ion arrays in various applications, ranging from quantum simulation to large-scale imaging. Moreover, the reversible logic-based circuit design method we employ offers advantages in terms of performance and efficiency. Notably, our results indicate that the accuracy of the hybrid scheme can be further enhanced if the postprocessing step incorporates a correction scheme to minimize measurement distortion. When humans operate robot arms, it is frequently necessary for the robot to infer the task the human is attempting to accomplish. Current research on assistive teleoperation and plan prediction focus on the human's physical movements, but these methods often lack the ability to explain the underlying task. This limitation makes it difficult for the human to understand the robot's adopted safety protocols and desired outcomes. This paper investigates a new approach, called T-InvEst, to improve invertible plan estimation through a new convergence-guaranteed algorithm. This is achieved by introducing an additional term to the optimization objective, to ensure that reconstructed plans closely resemble original plans. Comprehensive experiments were conducted using a DLR-III robotic arm to compare T-InvEst with a current state-of-the-art plan prediction method, E2F-SDP, showing that T-InvEst resulted in significantly higher inverse plan accuracy and reconstruction rates. This is a notable accomplishment, as previous studies primarily focused on short sequence reconstruction of 5 or 10 steps. Importantly, the findings demonstrate that T-InvEst can effectively communicate reconstructed plans to the human operator, and that this communication can enhance the human's understanding of the robot's safety protocols and desired outcomes. The study of light propagation within metallic areas is facilitated by a simplified model that reduces the complex electromagnetic fields to a local function driven by the field in a nearby zone. While this model is effective for understanding the scattering of light at a microscopic level, it has its limitations when applied to resonant metal structures that harness light through localized oscillations. The model's failure in this context leads to the emergence of 'divergent' behaviors, such as the accumulation of fields within small gaps. The present study aims to clarify these 'divergent' behaviors by examining the principles of electromagnetism and providing a more accurate description of light propagation using a refined model based on the quantum-mechanical concept of current.

The theory of light propagation in resonant metal antennas has been revised to address two critical issues. The first was the explanation of 'divergent' behaviors using simplified electromagnetism, leveraging the analogy between fields and potential to characterize dipole oscillations. The second involved developing a quantum-mechanical model to describe current and field behavior, which is capable of capturing the complex interactions between electromagnetic fields and metal resonators. The quantum model was applied to a family of ideal metal gratings, allowing for an insightful analysis of light propagation within the resonant structure.

The quantum model provides a straightforward description of light propagation, is applicable to both classical and quantum light sources, and reveals the inherent wave-particle duality of the electron traffic. The model's predictions coincide with those from a refined model based on classical electromagnetism, underscoring the efficacy of the quantum model in describing light propagation within resonant metal antennas. The quantum model's failure in replicating the behavior of the local model, however, indicates that 'divergent' phenomena should be treated as signs of wave-particle duality, which need to be correctly interpreted in capturing light propagation at the quantum level. The study of light propagation in resonant metal antennas serves as an apt platform for exploring the connections between quantum-mechanical concepts and classical electromagnetism. The quantum models' ability to explain 'divergent' behaviors provides a novel approach to understanding and fine-tuning light propagation within resonant metal antennas. Additionally, the quantum models' relevance to quantum information studies is worthy of further investigation.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by adjusting the position of the second YSR state, good agreement between theoretical and experimental results was achieved for both the Mn monomer and the first pair of the second YSR state. However, for the second YSR state associated with the second atom of the Mn dimer, reduced spin polarization on nearby Nb atoms was observed in contrast to the monomer case. This reduction in spin polarization for the second YSR state is due to depopulation caused by the finite overlap between the two YSR states. Moreover, a new method for calculating the spin dependence of the Hamiltonian based on specific parameters was employed. This parameter, indicating how much a magnetic impurity influences the superconductor, can be termed the "coupling strength" between the magnetic impurity and the superconductor. By employing this parameter, the theoretical spectra were able to accurately match the observed experimental outcomes. This theoretical framework is versatile and can be generally applied to the analysis of other magnetic impurities on the surface of superconducting materials. Furthermore, these theoretical models can be readily incorporated into a more advanced quantum simulation platform for future integration. In the future, this theoretical framework can also be further expanded to analyze and assess the coherent tunneling properties of hybridized magnetic impurity--superconductor states. Consequently, future development and incorporation of these theoretical models into a quantum simulation platform is also anticipated. This anticipated incorporation is also with the goal of achieving accurate simulation of quantum phenomena and to ultimately tackle quantum-like challenges in electronic transport. Subjecting solid materials to an ultra-intense, femtosecond X-ray pulse from a free-electron laser causes drastic electronic excitation, triggering rapid changes within the material's electronic system that unfold over the duration of the pulse. The amount of X-rays absorbed by the material becomes contingent upon the energy flux, giving rise to a unique form of X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy. Researchers can study valence excitation on the picosecond time scale with this type of XANES, providing insights into the dynamic changes in the valence excitations resulting from electronic relaxation processes. However, to accurately predict the spectral changes seen at high fluences, it is necessary to consider two distinct processes: the initial instantaneous response, influenced by the electronic wave function following a short (sub-femtosecond) period of intense excitation, and the post-relaxation changes, determined by the electronic population following longer (femtosecond or picosecond) time scales of electronic relaxation. Studies of strong electronic excitation in solid materials, typically applied in the context of high-fluence XANES, have resulted in altered valence excitations displaying shifted and broadened peaks, along with emission of copious secondary electrons. The application of a Deep Neural Network in Automatic Modulation Classification (AMC) exhibits enhanced performance compared to traditional methods even in harsh wireless environments, but this can be compromised by targeted adversarial attacks that inject noise into wireless channels. This paper presents a new method based on a generative adversarial network (GAN) designed to mitigate the effects of such attacks by removing malicious interference before feeding data into a DNN-based classifier. The proposed approach specifically protects AMC systems from attacks like the Fast-Gradient Sign method. The existing GAN defense algorithms were found to either fail in this context or substantially reduce the classifier's efficiency, whereas the presented strategy achieves a high AMC accuracy of 93.8% even when subjected to adversarial noise, whereas without this GAN defense the AMC accuracy would be significantly lower at 50%. It's worth noting that this GAN defense algorithm incurs a minor loss in BER performance of 0.5% compared to the scenario where no attack is present. Furthermore, the proposed GAN defense algorithm offers advantages over traditional methods like Maximum Likelihood Ranch (MLR) and the Deep Neural Network (DNN) based approaches in terms of reduced complexity by 42% and improved processing capacity by 65%, respectively. Overall, the presented GAN defense algorithm demonstrates an improved balance between AMC accuracy and system overhead. The research findings are verified through simulations conducted using the open source PyTORCH, PyTorch, and PyMNIST tools. A future perspective is also outlined. The paper is further supported by additional material including code at https://github.com/MultimodalAsso/GAN-AMC. Our goal with parameter-efficient tuning is to minimize updates to model parameters
when adapting a pre-trained model to downstream tasks. This paper proposes PASTA,
where we adjust only the special token embeddings, like separator and classification tokens in BERT, just before self-attention operations in each Transformer layer.
By doing this, PASTA can achieve performance on par with fine-tuning for natural language understanding tasks such as text categorization and question answering, all while updating a minimal number of parameters – just 0.0006% of BERT-Dropout's parameters. Notably, PASTA outperforms expert-guided tuning, which updates specific model submodules, and robustly leads with larger pre-trained model architectures.
